#3401. Robert Pattinson’s Crime Thriller Is Still His Greatest Movie 9 Years Later

Conor Sheeran is a Movies and TV features writer for Collider. He has a deep passion for cinema and watches everything from the biggest blockbusters to the smallest indies. While he specializes in movies and television, he has also written about politics, culture, and sports throughout his career. Based in New York City, Conor is also a massive fan of the New York Jets, Mets, and Knicks. He is still waiting for any of those teams to bring home a championship in his lifetime. A member of the National Writers Union and the International Federation of Journalists, Conor is a strong proponent of press freedom and collective action.

With the recent announcement of his casting as James Bond, it's clear that Robert Pattinson has had a pretty good few years. Since 2020, he's portrayed Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' The Batman; appeared in two Christopher Nolan films, The Odyssey and Tenet; and garnered massive critical praise for performances in movies like The Drama, Primetime, and Mickey 17. While he had once been known mainly for his starring role in the Twilight franchise, he has emerged as one of Hollywood's best actors. But even amid this run of incredible performances, his greatest role remains the one that arrived nearly a decade ago.

Released in 2017, Good Time, directed by Josh and Benny Safdie, is a relentless, anxiety-inducing thriller that centers on a small-time criminal who, after a failed robbery, attempts to rescue his brother. Set in a grimy and disturbingly unromantic New York City, Good Time is a nightmarish descent into the criminal underworld, a landscape where desperation, violence, and self-destruction are commonplace. Though Pattinson has become even more well-known for his turns in some of Hollywood's biggest films, his performance in Good Time was his finest role, and one that has yet to be beaten in his filmography.

On the surface, the premise of Good Time is straightforward and has few complications. Pattinson's Connie Nikas, along with his intellectually disabled brother Nick (Bennie Safdie), attempts to rob a bank. The heist goes wrong almost from the start, and when Nick is arrested and sent to jail, Connie pulls out all the stops to get the money together to bail him out, regardless of the consequences.

Pattinson’s entire career has been building to Bond.

Much like one of the Safdies' other films, Uncut Gems, Good Time is relentless in its tension, drama, and thrills that have you on the verge of a heart attack throughout. Connie's journey through New York City on his desperate quest to free his brother is equal parts frustrating and devastating. Every decision he makes as he traverses the city only seems to make his situation worse, pulling him into more dangerous problems with hardened criminals and complete strangers.

The film unfolds with the momentum of a 100-minute panic attack, never letting you catch your breath or process what you just watched before it jumps into the next disastrous development. Its close-up shooting style and claustrophobic framing pull you right into the drama and feel genuinely suffocating. There is something uniquely exhausting about watching Connie operate. Like the viewer, he never pauses to think about what is happening; he is always moving, talking, and searching for a way out. However, much like a man trapped in quicksand, the quicker he moves, the deeper he sinks into the consequences of his actions.

What truly elevates the movie beyond its already exceptional filmmaking is Pattinson's performance. For a long time, Pattinson was brushed off as "the Twilight guy," but it was films like Good Time that helped him shake off that perception and show general audiences his true, vast range. Connie is hardly a likable protagonist and is anything but conventional, much less a person anyone should admire. For all the love he has for Nick, Connie is selfish, manipulative, and cruel, someone who is willing to exploit nearly everyone he comes across to accomplish what he's set out to do.

Pattinson's performance is built around this fascinating dichotomy: a personality that makes little sense, yet you can tell he genuinely loves his brother. He's resourceful yet incompetent, someone who is selfish and selfless while using what street smarts he has to escape danger without considering larger consequences.

The actor captures these contradictions with impressive skill, a test that many other actors would fail. His frantic physicality, aggression, and ability to shift from charm to intimidation at a moment's notice make him feel like a real human and not a caricature. At times, it's almost easy to forget you're watching "that guy from Twilight" as Pattinson disappears into this character with his bleached hair and disheveled appearance. He is so far removed from a polished romantic lead that you start to question whether it's truly the same performer.

Since the premiere of Good Time, Pattinson has become even bigger than he was at the height of the Twilight era. He is set to play James Bond, he's Batman, and he is a frequent potential nominee for numerous Academy Awards. For all the good he does now, it was films like Good Time that first showed audiences what he was made of.

Nearly a decade after its release, the movie remains an extraordinary achievement, not just because of its incredible direction, narrative, and cinematography, but because Pattinson delivers a performance that continues to define his abilities. He may have become James Bond, but Connie Nikas remains his most unforgettable creation.

Good Time is streaming free on the Roku Channel.

#3399. Wendy Williams' 2007 Talk Show Contract, Salary Revealed In Court Battle

Wendy Williams was pulling in over a million dollars in her first year hosting her legendary talk show ... this according to documents filed in connection with a lawsuit brought by her ex.

The contract, executed on November 5, 2007, was submitted as evidence in the legal battle between Wendy's ex-husband Kevin Hunter and producers on "The Wendy Williams Show."

Per the deal, Wendy was paid $5K per week for the first 6 months of her test period ... but her salary jumped to $11K per week during the last 6 months of the test period.

Once the show was picked up, Wendy was paid a base salary of $1.25 million for hosting.

The fee went up to $1.31 million for the second season, $1.38 million for the third season, and was to be around $1.5 million for the fourth season.

The deal also provided for Wendy to receive 15% of the net proceeds from the show after the show recouped her base salary. The deal said the producers had full creative control over the series, as long as they "meaningfully" consulted with Wendy.

In 2012, Wendy's husband worked to renegotiate her contract. He asked for a $200K signing bonus and for Wendy to be paid $2 million for season four plus an additional $350K … much higher than she was set to receive under the initial contract.

He asked for Wendy to be paid $3 million in year five, $3.5 million in year six, and $4 million if the show went to season seven.

As TMZ previously reported, Wendy's talk show ended in 2022 due to the entertainer's health issues. The former talk show host is currently living in an assisted living facility in New York.

The two newest models face off with everyday tasks

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google and OpenAI are going head-to-head again, and this time, their newest AI models arrived just five days apart.

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, promising faster responses, stronger reasoning and better performance across everyday tasks. Then, on November 17, OpenAI fired back with GPT-6.2 Astra, its latest model designed to tackle everything from complex research and writing to coding and creative projects.

Both companies are making big promises about what their AI can do, but benchmarks and launch demos only tell part of the story. What matters is how these models perform when you actually put them to work.

So I put Gemini 4 Hydrogen and GPT-6.2 Astra through the same five real-world challenges to see which one delivers better results, where each struggles and which AI is actually worth using.

Prompt: You're an event coordinator managing a one-day technology conference with 120 attendees, three meeting rooms and six speakers.

The conference runs from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Each speaker must deliver one 45-minute presentation. Every presentation requires a 15-minute room reset afterward.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Speakers C and D must not present at the same time.

Speaker E must present immediately after Speaker A, in the same room, allowing for the required room reset.

Speaker F is available only between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.

All attendees must have a shared lunch break from noon to 1 p.m.

Each room can host no more than three presentations.

A 30-minute keynote involving all six speakers must take place at 4:30 p.m.

Create a complete conference schedule showing start times, end times, room assignments and speakers. Identify any conflicts and explain how you resolved them. Do not change any constraints without explicitly stating why.

GPT-6.2 identified both keynote conflicts, and it also identified the exceptions that would need approval. This directly addresses the instruction not to change constraints without explaining why. It correctly scheduled the six individual presentations and showed reset periods explicitly and preserved the shared lunch break.

Hydrogen was strong on presentation and the mechanics of the individual talks. Its table is easy to follow, with resets alongside each presentation. It also correctly handles the A-to-E sequence, B’s earliest start, C and D’s separation, F’s individual talk, lunch, and room limits. It also explains why the selected times work for the individual presentations.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins on constraint reasoning and transparency. Hydrogen offers a solid schedule, but it mistakes fitting the individual presentations into the day for satisfying the entire conference specification.

Prompt: Write the opening 500 words of a literary mystery novel. A woman arrives at a small coastal town to attend the funeral of someone she has never met. Everyone in town recognizes her, but nobody will explain why.

Start with a sentence of exactly seven words.

Include a conversation that sounds natural but contains a hidden threat.

Establish a distinctive setting without using a long descriptive paragraph.

Introduce one seemingly insignificant object that becomes important in the final sentence.

Do not use the words "mysterious," "secret," "shadow," or "dark."

End with a revelation that changes how the reader understands the opening.

Avoid clichés, melodrama and obvious AI-generated prose. Prioritize believable characters and original storytelling.

GPT-6.2 delivered an opening sentence that satisfies the seven-word rule and it introduced the identity question without explaining it. The narrator feels like a believable person and the setting emerges through activity. The threatening conversation retains plausible deniability. Alan’s questions about whether anyone expects her back could be concern or an assessment of how easily she could disappear. “If you get a signal” sharpens that uncertainty. That said, the ending is overcompressed.Hydrogen provided a clear, accessible opening with an easy-to-follow progression from ferry to town to diner. Its opening sentence also contains exactly seven words: “The morning ferry docked at eleven sharp.” It maintains first-person, past-tense narration and avoids the prohibited words. Hydrogen’s main weakness is that the final revelation does not sufficiently change our understanding of the opening.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins for an ending that makes the reader reconsider what already happened. Hydrogen’s ending mainly makes the reader wonder what happens next. Both can create suspense, but GPT-6.2 answers this prompt more successfully.

Prompt: Build a fully functional, interactive website called "Decision Lab" that helps people compare difficult choices.

Users should be able to enter up to five options, define their own decision criteria, assign importance weights from 1 to 10, and score each option against every criterion.

Automatically calculate weighted scores and rank the options.

Display a visual chart comparing the results.

Let users edit or delete options and criteria.

Include a sensitivity analysis showing whether the winner changes when the most important criterion's weight is reduced by 50%.

Include a "What if?" feature that lets users adjust weights and immediately see updated rankings.

Provide three realistic sample decisions that users can load instantly.

Save user changes between sessions if the environment supports persistent storage.

Use a modern, polished interface with intuitive controls. Every button and calculation must actually work.

Don't create a static mockup. Build the functioning app, then test its calculations and interactions. Explain any limitations.

GPT-6.2 built and published an interactive website for comparing up to five choices. I simply enter what matters, give each criterion a weight, and score the options. The site ranks them and updates the chart as changes are made. It also added a “what if?” slider section to experiment without changing original weights.

Hydrogen built a self-contained, responsive web application and tested its calculations and controls before displaying it. It also build a scoring matrix, added support for up to 5 options and implemented live calculations and charting.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins for a more thorough and useful website. The interactive site followed the prompt exactly while also adding extras that were useful for the overall project.

Prompt: You're the operations manager of an independent bookstore.

It's 4 p.m. on Friday, and the following problems happen simultaneously:

A bestselling author is arriving at 5 p.m. for a signing attended by 80 customers.

The shipment containing 60 copies of the author's book is delayed until Monday.

Your only experienced employee just called in sick.

A customer claims they were charged twice for a $75 purchase, but your payment system is offline.

A local journalist is asking whether the store is experiencing financial difficulties.

Your landlord has emailed demanding an overdue $2,000 payment by Monday.

You have $900 in available business cash, two inexperienced employees and one hour before the event.

Rank problems by urgency, explain what you would do in the first 15 minutes, write a short statement for customers attending the signing, and draft a response to the journalist.

You cannot cancel the event, invent money, pretend books have arrived or promise refunds that you cannot verify.

Be transparent without creating unnecessary panic. Explain what information you still need before making irreversible decisions.

GPT-6.2 treated the task as several connected operational problems, rather than simply a shortage of books. It prioritized safe event operations and gave inexperienced staff narrow roles. It checked capacity, kept exits clear, and assigned responsibility for the queue to better manage 80 attendees without the experienced employee.Hydrogen was practical in several aspects. But it promised to put bookplates into books “as soon as the boxes arrive Monday.” That turns the expected shipment date into a firm fulfillment commitment. Overall, the model introduced several unsupported assumptions — and its customer statement promises arrangements that its own plan says still need confirmation.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins as the stronger operations-manager answer because it preserved options while keeping customers, staff, the author and the landlord informed. Hydrogen had useful ideas but repeatedly moved from “ask whether this is possible” to “tell customers this will happen.”

Prompt: Five researchers, Ava, Ben, Chloe, Daniel and Elena, each work on a different project (robotics, climate, medicine, astronomy and cybersecurity), use a different programming language (Python, Rust, JavaScript, Go and Julia), and work on a different floor (1 through 5).

Determine each researcher's project, programming language and floor using these clues:

The robotics researcher works on floor 5.

The person using Rust works exactly one floor above the climate researcher.

The cybersecurity researcher works on floor 1.

Elena works exactly two floors below the robotics researcher.

Chloe does not work on robotics or climate.

Produce a complete table showing every researcher's floor, project and language.

Explain whether the clues produce exactly one solution, multiple solutions or no solution. If the puzzle is inconsistent or underdetermined, identify the problem rather than inventing an answer.

GPT-6.2 followed the prompt’s most important instruction. It identified inconsistency rather than inventing a complete assignment and it provided three clear ways to demonstrate the problem.Hydrogen reached the same correct conclusion and explained the same underlying problems. It successfully identified three contradictions and flagged the Floor 3 collision between Ava and Elena, the project–language mismatch on Floors 3 and 4 (medicine/Python and astronomy/Julia vs. Rust and Go), and Chloe being forced onto Floor 1 with no lower floor available for Ben.Winner: Hydrogen wins narrowly on clarity, accuracy and presention.

Google and OpenAI are competing to become your everyday AI assistant, but how each one handles tasks can make all the difference. In this experiment, GPT-6.2 won nearly every test, which might just make it one worth paying for. Hydrogen is free and did a decent job answering each prompt, but often struggled with assumptions and adding details. For users hoping to keep costs down, Hydrogen is still a good choice, you'll just want to do some extra fact-checking and evaluate the model's response a little closer than you would with GPT-6.2. Overall, GPT-6.2 proves to be a strong model for taking on every day tasks thoroughly, accurately and quickly. Have you tried these models yet? Let me know in the comments what you think of each one.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

#3396. Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security …

The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple launched Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

For myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

#3393. Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

#3390. 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. #3388. Florida Set To Execute 71-Year-Old Man Who Claims He Was Framed For Killing Pregnant Woman, Husband

Florida is gearing up for a record-breaking 20th execution this year ... but the man set to be put to death Thursday evening has spent decades claiming he was framed for the brutal murders of a pregnant woman and her husband.

Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection right now at Florida State Prison ... more than 35 years after Michael and Susan "Missy" MacIvor were found murdered inside their Florida Keys home.

And here's the twist ... Overton has insisted for years that he didn't commit the murders, claiming police planted the DNA evidence used to convict him. His attorneys have also raised some questions about how that evidence was handled.

The case dates back to August 22, 1991, when Michael, 30, and Susan, 29, were found dead inside their home in Tavernier, Florida. She was eight months pregnant at the time.

According to court documents, Michael had been hit in the head and strangled, with masking tape covering his face. Susan was found bound with tape and strangled in the couple's bedroom, and investigators determined she had also been sexually assaulted. The couple's unborn baby also died.

Investigators say they discovered the home's telephone wires had been cut and a ladder was positioned against the balcony.

The murders went unsolved for years ... until investigators connected Overton to the crime through DNA evidence.

According to court records, investigators recovered semen from the couple's bedding and developed a DNA profile in 1993, but didn't have a suspect to match it to.

That changed in 1996, when investigators arrested Overton in an unrelated burglary case. Although he initially refused to provide a blood sample, investigators eventually obtained a court order to collect his blood for testing. Two separate laboratories then reported DNA results linking him to the semen found at the crime scene.

But Overton has always insisted he was innocent.

During his original sentencing proceedings, he told the judge, "I didn't commit the crime." But he didn't present evidence that could have helped him avoid the death penalty because he said he believed his conviction would eventually be overturned on appeal and didn't want to put his family and friends through the ordeal.

In his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court, Overton's attorneys argued that more DNA testing could potentially clear his name or identify someone else involved in the murders.

His defense also claimed police planted the semen evidence to frame him ... and pointed to some unusual details about how investigators handled the evidence.

Overton's lawyers also argued the serologist assigned to the case took crime scene evidence home, stored biological samples in his refrigerator, and even drove a mattress pad to a psychic for an inspection.

Overton's attorneys also pushed to have hairs found on tape that was used to bind Susan tested for DNA, arguing the hairs didn't appear to match Overton or either victim and could potentially point to the true perpetrator of the crime.

Despite those arguments, the Florida Supreme Court rejected his challenges, finding the defense hadn't established that the evidence was tampered with or that the additional testing justified relief.

Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder, killing an unborn child, burglary, and sexual battery. He was sentenced to death.

Now, more than three decades later, Overton is set to become the 20th person executed in Florida this year ... breaking the state's previous record of 19 executions in 2025.

#3387. The 10 Most Inspired Oscar Wins of All Time, Ranked

Every young person with a dream for Hollywood has certainly pretended what it might feel like to win an Academy Award. They’ve held a hairbrush as a microphone, a shampoo bottle in hand, practicing their speech in front of the bathroom mirror. Many of those speeches come from those they have watched win on their TV. Whether it was an expected win or a massive shock, many inspiring victories have shaped generations that followed. We’re here to celebrate ten.

From groundbreaking firsts to sweeps that reshaped the landscape of the awards and movies at large, these ten inspiring wins have stayed with us long beyond their speeches. While many other groundbreaking Academy Award wins changed Hollywood, these ten represent a well-rounded mix of categories, eras, and legacies. Whose Oscar win made the greatest impact on you?

The history and legacy of songs in films leave a very different impression than the movies they came from. Not only can we enjoy them on their own, but they also bring us back to that moment when we heard them on the silver screen. For a long time, the Best Original Song winners maintained a specific essence and style. Then the 21st Century came and the times had changed. Once Eminem won for “Lose Yourself,” the door was open for Three 6 Mafia to win for “It’s Hard Out Here for a Pimp.” Winning for the film Hustle & Flow, the song emerged victorious as it captured the grit, struggle, and ambition of the film's main character, DJay (Terrence Howard), in a way that resonated emotionally.

The hip-hop group’s victory didn’t come as a shock for defeating Dolly Parton, but because of how it proved that independent, underground Southern hip-hop artists could reach mainstream Hollywood success without compromising their roots. Coming out of Memphis, Three 6 Mafia was an unlikely contender in a traditional award show setting, making their victory feel like a win for "outsiders.” They became the first hip-hop group to win an Academy Award and perform at the ceremony, making the night’s milestone even sweeter. Members Juicy J and DJ Paul didn't expect to win and had no prepared acceptance speech, but their enthusiasm reverberated through the room.

If there’s one thing that Bob Fosse is, it’s specific. Though he had been in the director’s seat in the past, his greatest cinematic triumph came through in his semi-autobiographical film All That Jazz. The legendary choreographer had a vision, and editor Alan Heim delivered. Though the Oscar went solely to Heim, Fosse collaborated quite closely with him in the cutting room. Heim and Fosse shaped the film with a driving, musical pace, blending theatrical choreography, rehearsal footage, and surreal sequences into a cohesive pulse. As Roy Scheider’s Joe Gideon nears physical collapse, the editing shifts fluidly between gritty backstage reality, hospital scenes, and elaborate musical fantasies.

Building on techniques discovered while editing Lenny, Heim moved fluidly across timelines and wove fantasy and dream logic into a straight narrative. This mirrors a mind under intense physical and creative strain. Techniques like cutting slightly off the beat or overlapping dialogue keep momentum high without feeling mechanical. Heim described moving time around and collaborating with Fosse as a creative adventure. Heim’s victory was a creative win. His win came against tough competition, beating heavy hitters including Apocalypse Now and Kramer vs. Kramer. The wildcard win showed how complex, long-gestating post-production can reward visual and rhythmic craftsmanship. Heim’s artistry is a benchmark of ambitious editing.

Sometimes playing yourself, or at least a version of it, can lead to massive success. For Diane Keaton, playing Annie Hall came as old hat, as Woody Allen modeled the titular character around her, name and all. Incorporating her natural mannerisms, humor, and tomboyish style was all it took as the Academy voters praised her fresh, self-deprecating comedic timing and nuanced portrayal of an awkward yet intelligent woman. Rather than playing a one-note "ditzy" character, Keaton balanced nervous tics and awkwardness with genuine intelligence and vulnerability. Her vintage menswear wardrobe of vests, ties, baggy trousers, and hats helped turn her into a defining late-1970s style icon.

Keaton’s victory for Annie Hall broke traditional conventions, celebrating individuality over traditional Hollywood glamour. Her candid, low-key acceptance moment stood out against overly scripted awards-show polish, making the win feel genuine and approachable. By redefining the leading lady through her achingly real presentation, Keaton influenced generations of performers and viewers alike. Sharp-witted, neurotic, and self-deprecating personas can be as equally charming as the formally polished presentation of a romantic damsel.

Before Get Out, most audiences knew Jordan Peele from his sketch comedy days. Then his directorial debut rattled cinema as a genuine Hollywood player. The film was a massive success, largely because of Peele’s groundbreaking original screenplay. Peele was awarded for writing an original horror-satire script that blended suspense with sharp social commentary on modern Black experiences. He combined psychological horror and satire into what he called a "social thriller," addressing themes underrepresented in mainstream horror cinema. Peele’s victory was monumental because he became the first Black writer to win the category. Only three other creators of color had been nominated in the category before him: Suzanne de Passé, Spike Lee, and John Singleton.

Shot in 23 days on a $4.5 million budget, Get Out proved that tight constraints and unconventional premises could yield major critical and commercial success. Peele framed the moment as part of a wider renaissance in Black filmmaking, encouraging young creators to claim their voices and tell stories that challenge industry norms. Peele shared in his acceptance speech that he stopped writing the script about 20 times because he doubted it would ever get made, yet kept returning to it because he believed people needed to hear and see the story. That part alone reminds anyone watching, no matter their craft, of the power of resilience. Coming from a low-budget debut by a writer-director best known for sketch comedy, Peele broke long-standing Oscar barriers for horror films and Black screenwriters. Underdogs rise up!​​​​​​​

When we examine the top-tier actors in cinema history, that list almost certainly includes Marlon Brando. His style of acting was on full display in On the Waterfront, and he was rewarded for it. He won the Academy Award because of his groundbreaking, naturalistic method-acting performance as dockworker Terry Malloy. His approach stood out as both intense and lifelike compared to traditional theatrical screen acting. The win marked Brando's fourth consecutive Best Actor nomination, signaling that Academy voters were ready to reward his sustained impact.

Brando’s performance paired working-class grit with quiet pain and moral awakening, most famously in the backseat cab scene in which he uttered, “I could have been a contender.” Brando was in quite a tough category, besting Humphrey Bogart, Bing Crosby, James Mason, and Dan O'Herlihy. Brando’s inspirational win validated emotional vulnerability beneath a tough exterior, influencing future elite actors including Daniel Day-Lewis and Joaquin Phoenix. Though Brando’s victory did not come as a shock, it was part of the film’s eight-award sweep that night. ​​​​​​​

Stanley Kubrick’s imprint on cinema is quite profound. Though his career includes many monumental moments, his victory alongside John Alcott for Best Cinematography is the most inspiring. Winning for the film Barry Lyndon, the victory came from its groundbreaking low-light filming techniques and a painterly visual style that recreated an 18th-century world without electric light. Capturing enough light in near darkness, Alcott and Kubrick used ultra-fast Zeiss Planar 50mm f/0.7 lenses originally created for NASA low-light photography. Exterior scenes relied on natural daylight and careful light control rather than heavy artificial setups.

The victory inspired future filmmakers because it proved authentic, period-accurate visuals could be achieved through daring technical problem-solving rather than standard Hollywood shortcuts. Principal photography took roughly 300 days across multiple countries, highlighting a close working relationship between a demanding director and a cinematographer willing to go the distance to achieve greatness. The win wasn’t undeserved, but rather shocking due to the overall sentiment regarding the slower, 3-hour period piece. While it competed against stiff competition like Jaws and One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest in other categories, there was no denying the inspiring influence of artistic creativity and ingenuity on the film’s cinematography.​​​​​​​

Firsts always have a massive impact, but Halle Berry’s monumental win for Best Actress was huge. For her role as Leticia Musgrove in Monster’s Ball, Berry was the first Black woman to win in that category. The win came to some as a shock, as the Golden Globes tend to be a predictor for the Oscars. She lost to Sissy Spacek for In the Bedroom. She won against a stacked lineup that included Dame Judi Dench for Iris, Nicole Kidman for Moulin Rouge!, Spacek for In the Bedroom, and Renée Zellweger for Bridget Jones's Diary.

In her acceptance speech, she dedicated the moment to "every nameless, faceless woman of color" and honored trailblazers and peers who shaped her path. She took on a demanding, low-paying dramatic part despite warnings about its difficult and explicit material. The role itself drew intense discussion around portrayals of Black women and female sexuality, but even with her win, Hollywood's casting habits did not fundamentally shift overnight. That same ceremony saw Denzel Washington win Best Actor, marking the only time both top acting Oscars went to performers of color in the same year. ​​​​​​​

Foreign language films rarely earned mainstream representation in the Best Picture category. When they do, it’s a formality and almost like a participation trophy. But then, one profound film walked away with the top honor: Parasite. Directed by Bong Joon Ho, the film earned the award because of its universal themes of class inequality, genre-blending craftsmanship, strong word-of-mouth among voters, and late-season awards momentum. It became the first non-English-language film to win Best Picture. Voters praised its tight structure, foreshadowing, ensemble acting, and seamless shifts between comedy, thriller, and drama.

Bong's win, echoing the idea that the most personal is the most creative, highlighted the power of distinct, auteur-driven storytelling. The win showed that non-English films and international creators can reach the highest level of mainstream awards recognition rather than be confined to international categories. It broadened global representation and encouraged viewers to explore cinema beyond Hollywood. While Sam Mendes’ 1917 entered the season as the clear frontrunner, the director’s charismatic campaigning, strong backing, and enthusiastic recommendations from voters helped overcome the traditional subtitle barrier. Now we celebrate foreign-language films as genuine contenders each year. ​​​​​​​

Sequels rarely get a chance for Oscar glory, let alone the third chapter of a franchise. Then The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King proved the naysayers completely wrong. Not only did the Peter Jackson adaptation have a good night at the 2004 Academy Awards, but it also swept all 11 of its Oscar nominations! Because The Fellowship of the Ring and The Two Towers had earned major nominations and technical wins without capturing Best Picture or Best Director, voters treated the finale as a cumulative reward for the entire trilogy, backed by a massive studio campaign that overcame longtime Academy bias against fantasy films. The Return of the King tied the all-time Oscar record held by Ben-Hur and Titanic.

Shooting an entire trilogy back-to-back over years was an unprecedented risk that reaped a beneficial reward. Winning celebrated a story rooted in courage, hope, friendship, and enduring human effort during a turbulent era. Fantasy had historically struggled to win top honors at the Oscars, making the clean sweep a watershed moment that helped break that barrier. What may come as a shock is that the massive achievement came even though none of the cast members received an acting nomination. ​​​​​​​

Horror rarely received a seat at the table. Then The Silence of the Lambs not only received an invitation, it was the true guest of honor. The film earned the rare honor of winning the “Big Five”—Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actor, Best Actress, and Best Adapted Screenplay. It became the third film in Oscar history to win all five major categories, joining It Happened One Night and One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. Jonathan Demme's direction emphasized psychological tension and character empathy over constant gore, working from Ted Tally's adaptation of Thomas Harris' novel. Jodie Foster as FBI trainee Clarice Starling and Anthony Hopkins, with roughly 16 minutes of screen time, as Hannibal Lecter, anchored the story with intense, memorable acting.

Defying the odds, its dark themes, cannibalism, and graphic violence felt far removed from traditional prestige Oscar fare. The Silence of the Lambs proved a dark thriller film could earn top-tier prestige rather than being dismissed as mere genre entertainment. Another shocker in its victory was its time of release. Coming out in February 1991, it won 13 months later—showing a film that did not need a late-year release to stay in the Oscar conversation. Though it faced off against massive contenders like Beauty and the Beast and faced protests outside the ceremony over its portrayal of killer Jame Gumb, controversy and competition were nothing for the massive hit.

#3386. Major websites compromised to steal crypto from iPhone users

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen …

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Several of the affected companies said that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme says almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

#3385. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3381. Now These Apple Services Are Down

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector shows user reports of issues across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially showed far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to users on Downdetector, there are currently outages or interruptions to the following Apple services, in order of most to least reported: Apple Support, Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music, Apple Store, Sign In with Apple, Apple Card. As of 1:44 p.m., Apple Support had the most reports, with over 13,000 user complaints. Comments suggest that users cannot log into their iCloud accounts, Apple Accounts, or activate devices, among other issues.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple says that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is currently unavailable. The company's System Status page shows an "issue" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

It's not clear what's causing the issues with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.

#3378. 8 Most Perfect Superhero Shows of the Last 15 Years, Ranked

Before superheroes took over cinema, they were extremely popular on television. For decades, they've been staples of the medium and have delivered some astounding content. Specifically, in the last decade and a half, superhero fans have been treated to some astounding content that has kept them engaged from year to year.

Whether they're from the likes of Marvel, DC Comics, or another studio, there have been some near-perfect superhero shows to air on both streaming services and network television since 2011. From animation to live-action, there are series that are about as close to perfect as one can get because of their writing, directing, visuals, and so much more.

When it comes to underrated television projects, one of the first projects DC Comics fans might think of is none other than Doom Patrol. Despite being in the same universe as Titans—a notoriously rough show—Doom Patrol was a great experience for those who watched it. The series takes the traditions of a superhero television show and decides to do its own thing.

Doom Patrol decides to center itself around a group of absolute misfits who are filled to the brim with trauma and complex characters. The world within this show is also bizarre and owns it. The best part, though? Doom Patrol manages to take the wacky and wild world, their traumatized characters, and bring them together. The way the show balances these two contrasting things makes Doom Patrol feel layered.

Superhero media is always a blast to enjoy when it's written traditionally, but Harley Quinn proves that a well-written satire can be just as effective—sometimes even more so. The Batman/Gotham City corner of the DC Comics universe has always been treated in a very grounded, gritty, and dark manner, which is why Harley Quinn ends up being as fun as it is. Using such a typically gritty world, and turning it into complete satire, leaves this 2019 adult-humored animated series being extremely hilarious.

But, that's not the main reason that the story finds itself being a pretty much perfect show—although it is a big part of it. Harley Quinn isn't fully focused on only being funny, but delivers heartwarming storytelling, too. It has a genuinely sincere plot that reminds audiences that it's not always about making people giggle, but truly affecting them emotionally, as well. Because of this, people have grown quite attached to the characters and want to continue seeing them on screen.

Finishing up the trilogy of shows that began in 2021 with WandaVision, Marvel Studios and Disney+'s VisionQuest has quickly become a certified hit. Following whom was once known as "White Vision" (Paul Bettany), this 2026 installment depicts the synthezoid not only starting to discover himself, but coming in contact with one of his two sons from WandaVision, Tommy Shepherd/Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). Not only that, but it features the return of the ever-popular villain, Ultron (James Spader).

Brought to life by directors Vincenzo Natali, Christopher J. Byrne, Terry Matalas, and Gandja Monteiro, VisionQuest's eight episodes weave together a phenomenal story. It doesn't just show the growth of Vision and Tommy, but shows the entire origin of AIs in the Marvel Cinematic Universe as a whole — which includes the classic Human Torch (Paul Bettany) featured briefly in Captain America: The First Avenger. No one could have ever guessed that AIs had such a wild origin back when they first met J.A.R.V.I.S. (Paul Bettany) in Iron Man, but VisionQuest makes it feel natural and believable.

In the last decade, one of the most popular anime in the West has become the one and only My Hero Academia by Kohei Horikoshi. Taking place in a world where the majority of the population has powers—known also as "Quirks"—this animated adventure depicts a young, quirkless boy named Izuku Midoriya (Daiki Yamashita and Justin Briner) gaining the power of the world's strongest hero, All Might (Kenta Miyake and Christopher Sabat). It's a bona fide underdog story through and through.

The numerous awards that My Hero Academia has won over the years—this last season being a prime example—is already the proof in the pudding that this show is the real deal. The animation is top-tier, the storytelling has excellent pacing, the character arcs are stellar, and the voice acting from both the Japanese and English casts is unforgettable.

Four teams, four completely different reasons to put yourself in danger for strangers. This is the roster you actually belong on, what they would want from you, and what it would cost you to stay.

You belong where the stakes are largest and the personalities are loudest. This is a team of people who are all used to being the most important person in the room, which is exactly why it works and exactly why it keeps nearly falling apart.

You have never had the luxury of being thanked for this. The X-Men protect a world that has never once been comfortable with them existing, and something in you understands exactly why they keep doing it anyway.

You do not want colleagues, you want your people. The Titans are the team where the friendship came first and the world-saving turned up afterwards as an inconvenient side effect.

You are not asking who to trust. You worked out the answer a while ago and it was nobody in a cape. This is where you go once you have decided the people in charge need watching, and that nobody else is going to do it.

Back when Avengers: Endgame premiered in 2019, no one could have expected the Loki (Tom Hiddleston) that escaped the 2012 timeline to have birthed one of the best superhero television shows ever made. Created by Michael Waldron, Loki is one of the most masterfully written superhero series in quite some time for numerous reasons that continue to prove why Loki is such a fan-favorite character.

Loki serves to be a great protagonist, giving Waldron the chance to truly delve into the concept of redemption in a way that is heartwarming and hopeful. Loki goes the distance by turning this classic villain into someone who is wholly relatable, cheer-worthy, and a true hero—arguably one of the best character arcs in the MCU, honestly. It also cannot be forgotten that the score, composed by Natalie Holt, is one of the best of the entire MCU franchise. Each track is mesmerizing, and it deserves all the praise it has gotten, and even more after that.

Some may think that a character as grand as Superman would be impossible to pull off on live-action network television. While that's more than a valid concern, given how straining network budgets can end up being, the unforgettable Superman & Lois managed to make a pretty much perfect Superman story with what they were given on a network like The CW. This show delivered not only a near-perfect Superman story, but one that feels incredibly unique among all the others in television and film.

In Superman & Lois, Clark Kent (Tyler Hoechlin) is married to Lois Lane (Elizabeth Tulloch) and has two sons, Jordan (Alex Garfin) and Jonathan (Jordan Eslass and Michael Bishop). Fans get to watch as Clark navigates being both a father and Superman, while his family grapples with the struggle of one of said sons getting powers of his own. Not to mention, for any fans of Inde Navarrette post-Obsession, this is one of her first major projects—playing Sarah Cushing—and, obviously, she kills it.

It's no secret that X-Men: The Animated Series is one of the most beloved animated series of all time. The impact it had on pop culture and the superhero medium as a whole rivals even that of Batman: The Animated Series. Few expected, however, that the show would somehow make a comeback. Thankfully, for X-Men fans everywhere, in 2024, they were treated to X-Men '97, which blew the world away by being the same level of quality as the original, somehow.

This continuation show is a perfect blend of what made X-Men: The Animated Series great and what modern fans of the series appreciate, while, at the end of the day, still managing to feel unique. Almost the entire original cast returns, the animation is updated while still feeling akin to the first, and they manage to evolve the story, without requiring audiences to watch through the entirety of X-Men: The Animated Series to get it. It's arguably the perfect example of how to make a follow-up series like this.

It's been said time and time again, and it doesn't become any less true: Daredevil is a work of art. Netflix and Marvel's television smash hit still goes down in history as one of the best superhero shows of all time, and, honestly, some argue that it's one of Netflix's best projects as a whole. Daredevil is a grounded, gritty, and raw story about the Man Without Fear that is engaging the entire way through. It introduced fans to some of the most iconic superhero castings out there, such as Charlie Cox as Daredevil, Jon Bernthal as Punisher, and Vincent D'Onofrio as Wilson Fisk.

After this series ended with its third season in 2018, audiences begged to see these characters again, which, in turn, spurred Marvel Studios and Disney+ to bring them back with Daredevil: Born Again. The best thing about this 2015 show is that even when it's at its lowest, it's amazing. Creator, writer, and developer Drew Goddard did a phenomenal job at bringing this Marvel Comics star to the small screen. The way the characters are developed across each season, and the dynamics they have with each other, is of the highest quality. While the plot is engaging from start to finish and the crime-thriller of it all is amazing, it's these amazing, well-developed characters that really serve as the best aspects of the show.

#3374. How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

#3371. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

If you're looking to find the best thriller movies to watch on Netflix this week, then you're in the right place. I've scoured the list of all the new movies that are arriving on the streamer this month and hand-picked three that I'll be adding to my watchlist.

This week's selection kicks off with a new Indonesian thriller that has taken the world by storm. We're following that up with a '90s action classic starring Harrison Ford. Then, finally, we're bringing it all home with a cult favorite in which Sylvester Stallone takes on the elements as well as gun-totting criminals. Can you guess which blockbuster we're talking about?

All three of these films deliver their fair share of action, surprises, suspense, and drama and are ideal for spreading out across the week. So, without further ado, let's take a look at the best Netflix thriller movies to watch this week.

This Indonesian action thriller has surprised everyone by becoming the No. 1 most-streamed movie on Netflix this week, charting in 89 regions around the world. It follows Hari (Lukman Sardi), a retired soldier haunted by the past and has retreated to a quiet life in the countryside. His isolation is broken when his son shows up and asks him to look after his two grandchildren. If that wasn't bad enough, it's at this exact moment that a crime syndicate chooses to come after Hari for revenge, forcing him to fall back on his military training to survive.

Directed by Sidharta Tata, "Never Surrender" transcends its — let's be honest — pretty predictable plot thanks to some excellent fight choreography, interspersed with heartfelt bonding between Hari and the two kids, Dimas (Sultan Hamonangan) and Putri (Callista Arum). If that sounds cheesy, then, yeah, it is a bit, but the cast are likeable and the action scenes exciting enough to make this more than worth your time.

Wolfgang Petersen's 1997 action classic delivers a stirring role for Harrison Ford as James Marshall, an ass-kicking Commander-in-Chief, who is called on to save the day when the presidential plane is hijacked by Russian terrorists. Leading the baddies is Gary Oldman, in fine snarling form as Egor Kurshonov (Gary Oldman) who threatens to kill everybody onboard unless terrorist leader General Radek (Jürgen Prochnow) is released from prison. Marshall fakes his escape and then does a "Die Hard": taking out the baddies one-by-one as he tries to stop Kurshonov and free his captured family.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

"Air Force One" was released in the same year as another beloved plane-based thriller, "Con Air". The two movies are quite different, however, with "Air Force One" delivering a more straight-down-the-line action movie than the Nicolas Cage-starring caper. Wolfgang Petersen is a master of taut thrills, as anyone who has seen his submarine-based masterpiece "Das Boot" can attest. "Air Force One" isn't quite that good, but it's a rollicking good time all the same.

It's fair to say that this Sylvester Stallone-starring survival thriller met with a mixed response when it premiered in 1993, with the legendary critic Gene Siskel describing the film as being "filled with howlingly bad scenes." He was not alone in that opinion. Over the years, however, "Cliffhanger" has become something of a cult classic – enough so that a remake is on the cards for early 2027.

Ably helmed by "Die Hard 2" director Renny Harlin, "Cliffhanger" follows rescue ranger Gabe Walker (Stallone), recently traumatized by the death of a friend in a mountaineering accident. Walker quits, but agrees to take on one last job: helping rescue the survivors of a plane crash, little realizing that they are actually deadly mercenaries, led by the psychotic Eric Qualen (John Lithgow).

Cue lots of jumping, swinging, and hanging vertiginously as the inaptly named Walker saves the day. Yes, "Cliffhanger" is silly, but it's also a huge amount of fun — and sometimes that's exactly what you want from a thriller.
