#3367. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Yesterday, Apple revealed that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for iPhone Duo on the App Store. That news came just ten days after the company announced that it had crossed the 100,000 milestone.

The Apple Store app was an odd omission from that category, but that’s now changed. The update comes as the holiday shopping season nears. Apple will likely announce its Black Friday promotion here in the next few days as well.

The update also adds a unified tab bar at the bottom, as well as a slightly different icon, as spotted by Everything-Apple.

You can download the latest version of the Apple Store app on the App Store. What are some of your favorite iPhone Duo apps? Let us know down in the comments.

#3365. Suspect in Custody After Making Threats At Same Campus Where Charlie Kirk Was Killed

A suspect is in custody after a man allegedly made threatening comments at Utah Valley University ... the same school where Charlie Kirk was shot and killed.

The University issued an alert a little before noon about comments that were made in the Keller Building, where the business school is.

The man reportedly made the comments around 11:45 AM and left campus shortly after. The school said in the alert there was no active threat on campus.

No word so far on what the so-called threatening comments actually were ... but UVU sent out another alert that afternoon saying the suspect had been arrested.

The suspect hasn't been identified, but police previously described him as 6 feet tall with blonde hair and wearing a beanie.

As you know ... Charlie Kirk was shot and killed while speaking at UVU on September 10, 2025.

#3364. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3363. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

#3357. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3356. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.

#3352. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

Thomas Markle didn't quite have his info straight during his court-ordered psych evaluation ... because he confused Meghan Markle and his other daughter.

According to the forensic psychiatric evaluation obtained by TMZ ... Markle told the psychiatrist that he only has one daughter, when he actually has two.

During the interview, Markle mentioned he had a son, Thomas Jr., and a daughter, Meghan.

The psychiatrist brought up Meghan's sister, Samantha, because he'd been staying with her, but Markle said ... "I don’t think so. I have two kids. I think Meghan is Samantha. I only have one daughter and one son."

At another point, when talking about his psychiatric history, he referred to Meghan as his "sister," before apologizing and clarifying that he doesn't have a sister and that Meghan is his daughter.

According to Page Six, Samantha went to a Tampa court Thursday to support her father in court, where a judge determined he's fit to stand trial.

#3347. iCloud, App Store, and other Apple services hit by ongoing outage [U]

Apple services are having a rough Tuesday. iCloud, the App Store, and other services are experiencing an apparent outage, with users reporting connection failures and trouble signing in.

Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.

Affected services include the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone Activation, and more.

Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.

Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.

Users are reporting unexpected iCloud sign-outs on iPhone and Mac, followed by verification failures or unknown errors when trying to sign back in.

Others say the App Store won’t load or download apps, while Apple Music and device activation are also running into problems. Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect.

The number of "coincidental" system failure happening these days make it difficult to believe it's not cyberattacks, AI failures, or both. Even more suspicious is that they all seem to be reciting the same script for the cause: "an internal update".

The disruption follows last week’s widespread Microsoft Outlook outage.

Yesterday, banking services also experienced problems after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online access and delayed some transactions involving other banks.

Are Apple services working for you? Let us know what you’re seeing in the comments.

Update: Apple now says an internal update caused the outage, ruling out a cyber attack, and many services are coming back online. Consumer-facing services are back online. Developer-focused services are still experiencing issues.

Apple: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.

#3345. The Google Wallet app is now available on iOS

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

The next tab shows a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”

The Black Friday mattress deals are live, making now a great time to pick up a new pillow for less. If the Saatva Down Alternative is on your radar this holiday season, check out my review in brief before you buy. Saatva is known for its supportive and breathable mattresses, so it’s no surprise that its Down Alternative Pillow offers a similar sleep experience. After a week of testing, I’d suggest it's one of the best pillows for side sleepers, especially those looking for a temperature-neutral and hypoallergenic night of sleep.

Type: Down alternativeBest for: Side sleepers, hot sleepersSizes: Standard Loft: 4-5 inches height, High Loft: 6-7 inches heightTrial: 45 nightsWarranty: 1-yearPrice: $95 at Saatva

The older I get, the more important a breathable pillow is to me. Considering how breathable Saatva’s mattresses are, it’s no surprise it brought that mindset to the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow. I never once got hot or sweaty sleeping on this pillow thanks to a cotton cover and a down alternative fill that allowed air to circulate through at night.

You can order the pillow in a standard or high loft size. I received a queen size in standard loft to test and it was about 2-3 inches taller than advertised. My head sunk more into the pillow when lying on my back, but not very much. The standard loft is a bouncy, plump pillow, and while it's not firm in the traditional sense, there isn't much give to the surface. I imagine this pillow will retain its shape for a good amount of time.

I slept most comfortably on my side with this pillow, even though it was just a tad too tall for me. Stomach sleeping isn’t possible with the Down Alternative Pillow, but if you like your head being slightly lifted when sleeping on your back, this pillow is for you.

It’s not the most comfortable pillow I’ve tested, but I think that has more to do with my body size not fitting with the pillow. I’m particularly glad it was hypoallergenic, as I tested it in the fall when my seasonal allergies were already triggered. Starting at $95, this pillow is on the high end for a down alternative pillow whose height isn’t adjustable, but at least it comes with a 45-day free trial.

The Saatva Down Alternative Pillow starts at $95 for a queen size in standard loft. Down alternative pillows are usually more affordable than this, ranging from $20-$75. If I had to guess, the price comes from the brand name more than anything else. We see the same pricing for similar down alternative pillows sold by Boll & Branch and SlumberCloud. I’d probably wait for a Saatva sale to grab this pillow; in its current Black Friday sale you can save $40 when you buy a pair of standard pillows.

At least Saatva offers a 45-night trial with free returns and a 1-year limited warranty for this pillow. The 45-night trial is longer than most pillow warranties, so that’s a good perk for the price.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Saatva Down Alternative Pillow is a breathable pillow with a cotton cover, hypoallergenic fill, and a bouncy, plump surface. Buyers receive a 1-year warranty and 45-night trial. The $95 price tag is somewhat high for a pillow made with alternative down, but during major sales you can often save when you buy a pair of pillows.

The Saatva Down Alternative Pillow is simply made. You can order it in two different lofts — standard or high — and in a queen or king size. The standard loft has a 4 or 5 inch height, while the high loft is 6 to 7 inches tall.

I received the standard loft size and when measured, it came out to a little over 7 inches tall. I can only imagine how tall the high loft option is.

According to Saatva, with the standard loft, you should be able to sleep in any position (including your stomach), while the high loft is better for side and combination sleepers.

The 100% sateen cotton cover has 400 thread count, and the interior is comprised of Versaloft recycled down alternative fibers. The recycled fibers make this pillow hypoallergenic.

Keep reading to learn more about how the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow performed over the course of a week of testing.

The Saatva Down Alternative Pillow arrived in a large cardboard box. Inside, I found the pillow zipped inside a white bag with handles. When I removed it from the bag, I didn’t notice any smells. The pillow was ready to sleep on immediately.

One look at the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow and I was pretty sure that I’d only be able to sleep on my side on it. Soon I discovered that I was right.

I tested the standard loft size, and as mentioned, it was a little over two inches taller than Saatva advertised. No wonder I found the pillow plumper and taller than the pillows I normally use. Upon lying on the pillow, my head barely sunk into the thick, bouncy surface. It did not contour around my head.

I placed a 15lb. dumbbell on the pillow, and it sank in about an inch. (The average weight of a head is 10-12 lbs.) Upon removal, the pillow bounced quickly back to its full size.

When lying on my side, my head didn’t sink into the pillow that much. However, when lying on my back, my head slowly sunk down a bit further, but not enough to really align my neck and spine. It was the kind of position that I like to be in when I’m congested or sick — with my neck and head tilted upward. Normally, however, I would not find that position comfortable.

I attempted to sleep on my stomach on this pillow, but I just slipped off. Since I can sleep on my side, I took up that position most nights, but unfortunately, I found that the loft (even the Standard Loft) was slightly too high to achieve a comfortable sleep. Perhaps my shoulders are too narrow.

That’s not to say that there is something wrong with this pillow, only that the width of my shoulders might not be long enough to fit this pillow when lying on my side. As the pillow softens over time, it could adjust into something that fits my body better. I think someone who is larger than me or at least broader in their shoulders, would like this pillow.

I’ve slept on down and alternative down pillows before, and I have to say that I prefer the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow because I suffer from allergies. The hypoallergenic nature of the pillow really aided me during testing since I was dealing with seasonal allergies and hay fever.

During testing, I didn’t get hot or sweaty sleeping on this pillow — which makes sense considering the materials. It’s filled with Versaloft down alternative fill: recycled fibers that allow air to flow through. The 100% cotton cover also played a role in keeping me cool and moisture-free overnight as it’s one of the most breathable materials on the market. While testing, I used a linen pillow cover which ensured I never once woke up hot.

No matter the pillow, you’ll probably need to replace it after two years. If your pillow resists being folded in half and bounces back quickly, there's still plenty of life left in it, otherwise, search for a new one as the fill has worn down.

I slept on at Standard Loft Saatva Down Alternative Pillow for a week and did not see any indication of the pillow sagging or lowering its loft. In fact, I kept hoping that the pillow’s loft would ease up a bit so I could sleep on it more comfortably, but that was never the case.

The pillow feels sturdy and durable, and I expect it to last you a full two years. The one-year limited warranty is fairly average across the industry.

Some people don’t realize that they need to care for their pillow to keep it in good shape and get their money’s worth. I’m glad to report that caring for the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow is easier than most.

For one, you don’t have to plump this pillow each day. It retained its shape as soon as I removed my head.

To get rid of stains or just to clean your pillow of the oils and fluids from your hair, face, or mouth, you can machine wash it on cold, as long as you do so separately from your other clothes. Once the pillow is done washing, Saatva suggests running an extra spin cycle to remove as much water as possible, since you’ll have to tumble dry the pillow on low until it’s fully dry (which could take quite a while).

The Saatva Down Alternative Pillow is a good choice for those with broader shoulders or who like a plump pillow that doesn't allow their head to sink in. That's not the kind of pillow experience I prefer, but I can't deny that there aren't some great qualities to this pillow.

It comes in two different loft sizes, so sleepers can choose the one that best fits their size and preference. Unfortunately I found the standard size to be taller (by 2-3 inches) than advertised, so keep that in mind when ordering.

The bouncy, supportive feel isn't firm, but the pillow won't let your head sink in when lying on your side or stomach, which are the most ideal sleep positions for this pillow (no matter what Saatva advertises).

A temperature-neutral sleep is the best thing the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow offers. You won't wake up sweaty or hot because the recycled fibers and cotton cover are so breathable and wick moisture away at night. Not to mention, the recycled fibers won't trigger any sleep allergies. If all that wasn't enough, you can also throw the pillow into your washing machine, making the care and maintenance for this pillow easier than others.

Truthfully, a $95 starting price is on the high end for a down alternative pillow, but at least the pillow comes with a 45-night trial with free returns which gives buyers some peace of mind.

✅ You're a hot sleeper: The cotton cover and down alternative fill makes this a very breathable pillow resulting in a neutral night’s sleep.

✅ You're a side or back sleeper: The higher loft (even with the standard loft size) and supportive feel makes it a good choice for side and back sleepers, especially since you won’t sink too much into this pillow.

✅ You have allergies: If you like the feel of a down pillow but hate waking with a stuffy nose, this down alternative pillow won’t trigger your allergies.

❌ You sleep on your stomach: While back and side sleepers could find comfort with this pillow, it’s too tall and doesn’t have enough give for stomach sleepers — which is why I slipped off every time I tried to sleep on my stomach.

❌ You have narrow shoulders: Most side sleepers will be supported by the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow, but since the pillow doesn’t have much give, it could be too tall for those with narrow shoulders.

❌ You want the ability to adjust your pillow height: The pillow may soften over time, but it’ll take months for that happen. If you prefer to adjust the height of your pillow from day one, like with the Coop Sleep Goods pillow, then the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow is not for you.

A $60 price tag feels a lot more realistic for a down alternative pillow, which is why you might consider the Beckham Hotel Collection Original Down Alternative Pillow. It’s a good choice for side and back sleepers and will keep you temperature neutral at night. Our reviewers aren’t as confident about its long-term durability, and they were disappointed by a lack of a sleep trial and warranty.

The Saatva Latex Pillow is one of our editor’s top picks for its breathability, comfort, and benefits for sleepers with allergies. The fill is made with shredded latex, which allows air to flow through at night. The cover is washable and you can order the pillow in two loft heights. It provides a huggable sleep feel so your head sinks in more compared to the Down Alternative Pillow. At $165, the Saatva Latex Pillow is more expensive, but may be worth the investment.

Those who don’t have allergies could consider the Helix Down & Feather Pillow. This plush and fluffy pillow is often discounted to $79, making it more affordable than the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow. It is better suited to side sleepers or back sleepers who like a higher loft, though interestingly enough, it has more of a sink-in feel resulting in a softer sleep experience. #3342. ‘The Hunger Games’ Is About Oppression and Sacrifice. Why Does Hollywood Market It With Luxury?

In author Suzanne Collins’ dystopian YA novel The Hunger Games, a reluctant teen revolutionary named Katniss Everdeen destroys a fascist government that broadcasts children fighting to the death for sport. The book makes pointed critiques of the fictional Capitol’s ruling class, constantly juxtaposing government-created poverty, violence, and forced labor with a cadre of one percenters whose lives are focused on high fashion, merriment, and excess. It’s a moral lesson served on a platter for middle-grade readers: Look for the bad guys — they’re the ones in the sparkling ball gowns, fat and happy while the protagonists suffer.

In the close to two decades since Collins published The Hunger Games in 2008, the now five-novel series has grown into a cultural phenomenon with 100 million books sold and a blockbuster film franchise. Out Nov. 20, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, based on the 2025 book of the same name, is the latest adaptation of Collins’ world to the screen — a prequel charting the heartbreaking life of Haymitch Abernathy before he was Katniss’ drunk mentor and friend. (Joseph Zada stars in Sunrise on the Reaping; in the original films, an older Haymitch is played by Woody Harrelson.) With new stars and the return of original cast members Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Harrelson, Sunrise on the Reaping has been positioned as the dominant big-budget film of the Thanksgiving holiday, enjoying months of promotional stunts, lavish influencer parties, international installations, and couture-themed red carpets. It’s a blitz of glossy promotion for the sixth film in the franchise and the second in under three years. So why is it, after all this time, The Hunger Games franchise still hasn’t figured out that its marketing misses the entire point of its films?

In Sunrise on the Reaping, Haymitch is chosen as one of District 12’s male tributes — sent with Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) to the Capitol to fight to the death in a deceptively pastoral arena. But while citizens of Panem revel in the mental games of sponsors, allies, and grievous bloodshed, Haymitch is drafted to be the linchpin of a secret District rebellion. If Katniss is a symbol later in the series, Haymitch is a blunt weapon in his standalone film — a devastating and tragic example that revolution often requires sacrifices from people who will never see the fruits of their labor. But you wouldn’t be able to tell that from Sunrise on the Reaping’s pre-release campaign.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

For Paris’ October Fashion Week, the studio behind the film, Lionsgate, held a Sunrise on the Reaping-themed costume exhibition at the sculpture garden of the Musée Rodin, a two-day experience titled “Elegance Is Authority: The Story, Style and Power of Panem.” Cast from the film attended the opening, complete with a six-course dinner incorporating themes for each of the 12 Districts, according to WWD. Outside the film’s promotional bubble, social media timelines were splashed with a viral video of a French orchestra playing the Hunger Games rebellion theme, “The Hanging Tree,” outside during the ongoing French student protests. (They only stopped when they were teargassed by police.) Cosmetics brand Stila was chosen as the official partner for the film and launched an accompanying makeup collection, including a “Sunrise Eyes Liqua-Play” shadow collection with shades “Maysilee,” “Lenore Dove,” and “Mags” named after women murdered by the Capitol. At this week’s New York premiere, attendees were encouraged to follow a “Make Them Remember You” theme for their attire — advice Haymitch gives to Katniss in the first film in an effort to help her survive. According to Vogue, people dressed in Capitol-inspired party outfits walked over to the official afterparty at the tony Metropolitan Club, which had been decorated with ice sculptures and Panem flags. Everything from television spots to posters, cast interviews, and fan events for the film has had this emphasis on spectacle and excess — a focus that completely ignores the story’s inherent social critiques.  Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Bruno Mars Mourns His Father's Death: 'The Man That Taught Me Everything I Know' Pearl Jam Plan ‘Big-Boy Conversation’ About New Drummer YouTube Rejects U.K. Government’s Request to Take Down Russell Brand Video Related Content Hear Ella Langley’s Reflective ‘Hunger Games’ Single ‘Here Then We’re Gone’ New ‘Hunger Games’ Novel Coming in 2025 From Suzanne Collins Where to Stream All the 'Hunger Games' Films Before You Watch 'Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes' 'The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes' Is One Stuffed (But Satisfying) Prequel

Sunrise on the Reaping isn’t the only Hunger Games film that’s fallen into this trap. There’s a consistent pattern of tone-deaf or straight-up ridiculous promotional attempts across the franchise. In 2025, Lionsgate announced a Hunger Games merch collaboration with fast-fashion company Shein — which fans balked at, considering the books’ themes about child exploitation and labor rights stand in opposition to the clothing giant known for its brutal working conditions. In 2014, for Mockingjay — Part 1, the Hunger Games promotional team released a version of “The Hanging Tree” titled the “Rebel Remix” — EDM tones and synth added to make the dirge fit for radio play. “Are you, are you/Coming to the tree?” a sped-up version of Lawrence’s voice sings, calling for rebels to fight the Capitol and “Wear a necklace of hope/Side by side with me.” (Yeah, seems fun to dance to.) Perhaps the most notorious example happened in 2013, when makeup brand CoverGirl launched its Capitol Collection, inspired by the best and richest looks in Panem. The backlash was so immediate that it inspired one the most longstanding memes on Tumblr — a parody Katniss Everdeen makeup tutorial with the instructions “we’re going to use a black eyeshadow to represent the coal mines that her father was smashed to death in.”

When Collins published A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020, her first Hunger Games book in a decade, she told her publisher she had returned to the story because she thought people were beginning to “lose sight” of the dangers of authoritarian rule and what it takes to slowly dismantle a democracy. It’s not a coincidence that younger generations are flocking back to dystopian stories — the ones publishers and studios alike were convinced were flagging — at the same time that they’re becoming more politically minded. Collins’ books and the films based on them present a fictionalized and desperate endpoint to totalitarian ideas; one that readers and moviegoers are treating as more important than ever. But in the promotion of these films, Hollywood not only misrepresents the message of its source material, but betrays a striking lack of faith in the rich world the series has built — and the viewers who believe in its power.

#3341. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

You can read more in OpenAI’s full announcement.

#3338. Fiona, Cincinnati’s Zoo’s Beloved Miracle Hippo, Has Died

In a turn of fate somehow sadder than Punch the Monkey’s isolation and crueler than the loss of Harambe, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday that the beloved, internet famous Nile hippopotamus, Fiona, has died at the age of 9.

“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a tribute Thursday. “We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are.”

Last week, vets reported that Fiona swallowed a knit hat that was accidentally thrown into her enclosure. Several days after the incident, Fiona’s appetite declined and zookeepers started a variety of tests and 24-hour care, in the hopes that Fiona could pass the hat naturally. (Surgery is a rarely recommended suggestion for hippos due to its high risk.) But Fiona continued to decline, losing energy and fluids.

“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” Thursday’s statement added. “Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.”  Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Bruno Mars Mourns His Father's Death: 'The Man That Taught Me Everything I Know' Pearl Jam Plan ‘Big-Boy Conversation’ About New Drummer YouTube Rejects U.K. Government’s Request to Take Down Russell Brand Video

Fiona made history when she was born in 2017 as the first hippo born at the Cincinnati Zoo in over 53 years. (She was named after the Shrek character, princess Fiona, for the unique shape and size of her ears). Her mother, Bibi, was 17 at the time and went into labor early, delivering Fiona six weeks premature. Fiona was only 29 pounds and could not stand or nurse on her own.

Keepers and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo began documenting her growth on social media, drawing in millions of well-wishers and international fans as they watched the wobbling baby hippo fight to live and then begin to thrive. Even when Fiona reached adulthood, she remained a beloved internet icon known for her strength and resilience through seemingly insurmountable odds. Fiona was a fighter — even until the end.

#3337. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3336. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3335. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.
