#3248. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on Smartwatches and Fitness Trackers

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but the early Black Friday sales are in full swing. I've been keeping an eye on all the best fitness trackers and smartwatch deals so that you can snag the best possible price from now until the end of Cyber Monday (Nov. 30). Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

The Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. These are the lowest prices ever for these rings, which usually go for $399 and $499, respectively. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I've tried, although it's worth noting it requires a $5.99/month subscription fee.

For an even cheaper deal, the older Oura Ring 4 is $249—a full $100 off its list price of $349. If you opt for "stealth" (matte black), the price is $279; for gold, it's $286.61, down from $399. While this model has since been replaced by the Oura Ring 5, it's still an accurate and comfortable smart ring—especially if tracking your sleep is your priority.

Whoop may be one of the most expensive smart bands out there, thanks to its subscription-only model. But that price is particularly low right now, since the Peak membership that normally goes for $239 is now $199. Peak is the middle tier, and it's the one I recommend. While you can get Whoop One for $189 in this sale, the $10 you save isn't really worth it given the features you'd be missing. I also wouldn't normally recommend Whoop Life, since its ECG readings and blood pressure estimates aren't really worth the extra $100+. That said, if you do want it, the Life tier is $299 right now instead of $359.

The new Luna band is on sale for $119.20, down from a normal price of $149. The Luna band is made by Indian smartwatch company Noise, the same company behind the Luna Ring that I reviewed last year. The ring is no longer available in the U.S., but the band is. It's a Whoop-style screenless fitness tracker, potentially a worthy competitor to the Fitbit Air and other smart bands.

This is the brand-new Apple Watch model, and it's actually worth the upgrade. One of the biggest reasons is that the Series 12's new processor (called, confusingly, the S11 chip) supports some features older Apple Watches can't, and a good rule of thumb is that whenever there's a break in software compatibility, it makes sense to get the newer model. Right now, I'm seeing it for as low as $329, down from the list price of $399. (And if you're stuck deciding between an Apple Watch and a Fitbit, Beth breaks it all down in her comparison of the two watches.)

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is Nothing's latest smartwatch, and it incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT; you can currently pick it up at a major discount. Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $55. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been.

If you're looking specifically for a sporty, outdoors watch, Garmin sets the standard. (You could definitely call me something of a Garmin enthusiast.) Here are the best Black Friday deals on Garmin watches that I've seen so far:

The 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 is 249.99 (down from $449.99). The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class—a must for those going off-grid.

The Garmin Fēnix 8 in titanium with a gray band is $749.99 (down from $999.99). While this is last year's model, it's a perfectly solid option if you don't specifically need the titanium case or the latest mapping engine in the latest Fenix 9 Pro.

The Garmin Forerunner 265 is $299.99 (down from $449.99). Although it isn't the latest and greatest anymore, this is still a fan favorite among Garmin users. It's a step above entry-level options, with dual-band GPS, power meter compatibility, and advanced analytics (like training status).

These aren't the only sales you'll see on fitness watches and trackers during the big shopping holiday; the following brands have announced they'll be launching more deals on Nov. 19:

Additionally, though the sale has ended, the Google Pixel Watch 5 was recently marked down by $100; I'll be keeping an eye on this device to see if that particular deal comes back once Black Friday officially arrives.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

For most people, the Apple Watch SE 3 at $199 is a good starting point, covering everyday fitness tracking, notifications, and essential health features without the higher price of the Series 12. If you want more advanced health monitoring and a more premium smartwatch experience, the Series 12 at $329 is worth considering.

Yes, Garmin is one of the best brands when it comes to rugged sports watches and fitness trackers. The Forerunner line especially, is a go-to pick for accurate and reliable GPS tracking for runners.

#3247. ‘Can’t Hardly Wait’ Stars Campaign For Sequel To 1998 Teen Movie: “Would Be So Fun”

After nearly 30 years, the cast of Can’t Hardly Wait is ready for a Huntington Hillside High reunion.

Having reprised their roles from the cult classic 1998 teen film for Halloween, Peter Facinelli and Joel Michaely noted that fans “have been clamoring” for them to make a sequel for years, suggesting they make their interest known to Sony Pictures.

“I brought Mike Dexter back for Halloween, and weeks later the internet is still talking about it,” Facinelli told TMZ of his bully jock character.

“A Can’t Hardly Wait sequel is the one high school reunion everyone actually wants to go to. Would be so fun to get the whole gang back together and see where they ended up,” he added. “If we’re lucky, LoveBurger might finally play a song — and maybe, just maybe, if I play my cards right I can finally get Amanda Beckett [Jennifer Love Hewitt] back.” Watch on Deadline

Joel Michaely, who played one of the “X-Phile” nerds, noted, “People have been clamoring for us to do a reunion movie for years. Now is the time for our 30th anniversary in 2028. While we all still look hot.”

“We need Sony to make it or partner with a streaming service like Netflix or Amazon, so tell them you want to see it,” he added.

In Can’t Hardly Wait, six high school seniors attend their grad night house party, where Preston Meyers (Ethan Embry) plans to give his long time crush Amanda (Hewitt) a love letter after their chance encounter four years before.

The star-studded ensemble also included Seth Green, Lauren Ambrose, Charlie Korsmo, Selma Blair, Jason Segel, Melissa Joan Hart, Jerry O’Connell, Donald Faison, Jaime Pressly, Clea DuVall, Leslie Grossman, Breckin Meyer, Sara Rue, Sean Patrick Thomas, Amber Benson, Marisol Nichols, Jennifer Elise Cox and more.

#3246. Instagram finally lets users edit Stories after publishing, but there’s a catch

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that users will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

#3244. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

#3243. ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Broadway Review: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell & Jamie Lloyd Throw An Irresistible Party Of Shakespeare’s Great Comedy

Outside of ticker tape parades and New Year’s Eve in Times Square, you might be hard-pressed to think of a better, more joyous use of floating paper than the confetti that piles up nightly on the stage of Broadway‘s Winter Garden Theatre these days. We’re talking blizzards of the pink stuff, so deep that the man known for playing that Marvel trickster Loki can all but bury his superhero frame in the drifts.

The new, infectious Much Ado About Nothing, Jamie Lloyd‘s inventive and joyous revival of the Shakespeare comedy opening tonight at the Winter Garden, turns those old falling drifts of thin paper into a special effect that, for sheer exuberance, more than holds its own against the cutting-edge projections and awesome digital flimflammery delighting audiences at any number of Broadway houses this season. Related Stories News Josh Radnor & Beth Behrs To Join Broadway's 'Schmigadoon!' News Jonathan Spector's Acclaimed 'Birthright' Sets Spring Broadway Opening

Of course, even a confetti squall such as this wouldn’t impress a lick if the rest of Lloyd’s production couldn’t match its energy, and fortunately for us all this Much Ado About Nothing never lacks for giddy enchantment, from the Tony-worthy performances of stars Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell to the irresistible choreography of Fabian Aloise that will likely leave audiences of this straight play convinced they’ve just witnessed one of the best new musicals on Broadway this season. Watch on Deadline

Hiddleston, with his charm level cranked, and Atwell, best known to moviegoers for her Agent Carter of Marvel fame and here matching her fellow superhero beat for beat, play Benedick and Beatrice, two of Shakespeare’s most delightful characters, Loki-level tricksters who, as another character notes, engage in a “merry war” of plotting, planning and scheming in the name of love (though neither would admit to that motive, at least early on).

Lloyd, whose typically stark theatrical approach if on full view here but utilized to an effect wholly different than the shadows-and-light desolation of his A Doll’s House (starring Jessica Chastain) or Betrayal (which also paired him with Hiddleston), fashions this foray into Shakespeare as a 1990s-era dance club – at one point, the entire cast dons oversized, mascot-style headpieces (a chick, an octopus, a dog, a robot and more) suggesting so many ecstasy-fueled club kids packed into the Limelight.

The plot, of course, is the usual Shakespearean farce full of disguised identities, battles of the sexes, intricate schemes and star-crossed romances both helped and hindered by busybodies, eavesdroppers and nefarious in-laws. (In Shakespeare’s day, the word “nothing” carried a double meaning: In addition to our understood definition, “nothing” in its ye olde pronunciation carried a near-pun on the word “noting,” or gossip).

While productions of Shakespeare have long been interpreted with any number of contemporary spins and modern touches – such are the stock in trade of New York’s Shakespeare in the Park – Lloyd has come up with an approach that feels entirely fresh: Hiddleston, Atwell, the wonderful Mason Alexander Park and the rest of the cast move and sing to such jubilant dance and pop hits as Taylor Dayne’s “Tell It to My Heart,” C & C Music Factory’s “Gonna Make You Sweat (Everybody Dance Now),” Deee-Lite’s “Groove Is in the Heart,” and All-4-One’s “I Swear.” I knew we were in for a treat when Hiddleston’s Benedick and his boy crew made an entrance dancing to the Beastie Boys’ booming “Fight for Your Right (To Party).”

If period drama set to a more-or-less contemporary soundtrack doesn’t sound all that innovative – Six and Moulin Rouge! would like a word – Lloyd and his crack creative team (and his cast, of course) see to it that we pretty much forget all other contenders. With that ever-present pink confetti, a giant inflatable heart, character-accentuating modern dress (Soutra Gilmour did both the scenic design and the party-wear costume designs) and Jon Clark’s gorgeous lighting combine to create a dazzling experience. Like any dance club worth its cover charge, the sound design (by Ben and Max Ringham) is practically a showstopper in itself, with music thumping when it needs to thump and, when we need to hear dialogue, dropping to the sort of low-level thrum you might hear on the curb outside a packed club.

Hiddleston, whose last team-up with Lloyd was the austere Betrayal, is a revelation here, adding some incredibly hot dance moves to his overflowing bag of tricks. And he’s very, very funny (watch how he ever so deadpan blows a bit of stray confetti from his lips), playing off his movie star appeal with every sidelong glance and knowing grin seemingly directed to each person in the audience (he’s not above a quick show of gratitude when his seated admirers whoop their appreciation, as if his Benedick is welcoming everyone into his scheming maneuvers).

Atwell is every bit his equal, with Beatrice’s fiery, feminist mettle rendered as the true heart and brains of this tale. Both actor and role are this productions not-so-secret weapons – and yes, Lloyd and his cast are entirely in on the Marvel appeal going on here, so much so that Hiddleston-as-Loki and Atwell-as-Carter make brief appearances in the form of standees that had the audience at the reviewed performance all but levitating.

As good as they are – and they are – newcomer (to American audiences anyway) Mason Alexander Park as the sharp-tongued Margaret nearly walks off with the show, never more so than when, mic in hand, she/they performs “Tell It To My Heart” as if placing a dance-pop diva in 16th Century Milan is no more strange than wooing your heart’s desire.

Indeed, there’s no weak link in this cast, with James Phoon’s callow young Claudio swoon-worthy when he needs to be, infuriating when he’s a jerk; Tim Steed’s meddlesome Don John a hissable villain; and Gerald Kyd’s Don Pedro – that fair-weather father to the slandered Hero (a winning Mara Huf) – an appropriately garrulous, welcoming host (until he isn’t).

The grand appeal of this production is evident in just how much Hiddleston, Atwell and their compatriots seem to be enjoying themselves, and why not? So is everyone within the clarion-call-to-groove of those thumping, galvanizing dance beats.

Title: Much Ado About NothingVenue: Broadway’s Winter Garden TheatreWritten By: Willliam ShakespeareDirected By: Jamie LloydCast: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell, Mara Huf, Mika Onyx Johnson, Gerald Kyd, Forbes Masson, Phillip Olagoke, Mason Alexander Park, James Phoon, Tim SteedRunning Time: 2 hr 20 min (including intermission)

But as their relationship becomes increasingly complicated and their business begins to unravel, they find themselves at the centre of an $8 billion financial fraud scandal.

Why you should watch it: This new series is worth watching if you enjoy scandal-driven dramas based on real events. Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle are great as the infamous crypto couple, bringing plenty of personality to a story full of money, bad decisions and betrayal. The rise and fall of FTX is already a pretty wild story, so there's plenty here to keep you hooked. Fans of "Inventing Anna" and "The Dropout" should definitely give this one a go.

What it's about: "Never Let Go" follows a mother (Halle Berry) and her twin sons, Nolan and Samuel, who live in isolation in a remote cabin, believing an evil force has taken over the outside world. To protect themselves, they must remain physically connected to their home using ropes whenever they venture into the woods. But when one son begins questioning whether the supernatural threat is real, their fragile family bond is pushed to breaking point, threatening their survival.

Why you should watch it: This horror has plenty going for it if you're in the mood for something creepy and unsettling. Halle Berry gives a strong performance, and the eerie woodland setting makes a great backdrop for its tense survival scenes. I also liked how the film keeps you guessing about whether the threat is actually supernatural or something else entirely. The ending doesn't quite work for me, but there's enough here to make it worth a watch for horror fans.

But when he discovers the treatment is an elaborate scam targeting vulnerable patients, he takes matters into his own hands. With the help of his apprentice Amanda (Shawnee Smith), John subjects those responsible to a series of brutal, elaborate traps in one of Jigsaw's most personal games.

Why you should watch it: "Saw X" is one of the stronger entries in the franchise, and Tobin Bell is a big reason why. He's fantastic as Jigsaw, while the gruesome traps deliver all the twisted moments you'd expect from a Saw movie. It also has a more personal storyline and the return of fan-favorite Amanda, which gives longtime fans another reason to tune in. It's a great pick if you enjoy your horror bloody, brutal and full of nasty surprises.

Watch on Deadline

“I’ve been in this universe for a while,” said Hewitt, who has played Maddie since Season 2 of 9-1-1 in 2018. “It’s such a safe, lovely place to be with the best people. And he and I have not seen each other since I was 18 years old.”

Having “never seen each other again” after wrapping the film, Hewitt noted that working together again “was a dream” and Phillippe “hadn’t — for me — changed at all,” adding that “he was the same in the most beautiful way.”

The upcoming 9-1-1 crossover with 9-1-1: Nashville comes amid the parent series’ 10th season and the spinoff’s sophomore season, airing back-to-back on Thursdays at 8/7c and 9/8c on ABC.

#3237. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3236. Anthropic IPO Live — everything you need to know about the $1.5 trillion AI giant

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, is officially entering an IPO with aggressive stock prices set at $83 share, though it's expected to begin trading at $110 per shared based investor interest.

The company recently reported third quarter revenue of $17 billion, the IPO values the company at trillions more.

At the same time, Anthropic's public stock debut comes at a strange time in the AI industry. Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang just resigned after accusations of affairs and being in a spy web.

AI stocks in general have taken huge hits in the last few weeks. Plus, Anthropic faces major competition from its main rival OpenAI as well as from Google and Meta.

Now the market will determine if Anthropic is as viable as CEO Dario Amodei thinks it is.

Anthropic may be worth more than $2 trillion, but the company behind Claude is offering some businesses discounts of more than 30% to keep them from switching to ChatGPT.

According to a new report from The Information, Anthropic is offering aggressive discounts and credits worth as much as $100,000 to encourage companies to adopt its growing lineup of AI products.

The catch? Some businesses must commit to spending a certain percentage of their overall AI budgets on Anthropic. The company has reportedly started requesting invoices and other documents to verify that customers are meeting those commitments.

It's an interesting strategy for a company celebrating a historic IPO. Claude Code helped Anthropic become a major force in AI, but the company now wants to bring Claude into more workplaces through tools for finance, marketing, human resources and cybersecurity.

That puts Anthropic in direct competition with OpenAI, Microsoft and Google, all fighting for a larger share of corporate AI spending.

For everyday Claude users, these discounts aren't necessarily coming to individual subscriptions. But the competition could eventually mean more capable AI tools and better pricing.

Anthropic now has a massive valuation to justify, and winning over businesses beyond software development could be critical to its next chapter.

Not everyone is celebrating Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. One AI CEO believes the company is making a massive bet on infrastructure that could eventually become obsolete.

David Stout, co-founder and CEO of webAI, is questioning Anthropic's valuation after the company priced its IPO at $83 per share.

"Anthropic's IPO asks public investors to bet that the future of AI belongs to whoever spends the most to centralize it," Stout said in a statement shared with Amanda Caswell.

His biggest concern is Anthropic's nearly $900 billion in computing and infrastructure commitments, some extending through 2045.

Stout argues that cloud-based AI becomes more expensive as people use it more, while AI running directly on phones, laptops and other devices could eventually offer a cheaper alternative.

"Anthropic is asking investors to pour billions into an infrastructure model that AI itself is making obsolete," he said.

There's an important catch to his argument. Smaller AI models are becoming more capable, but running the most powerful models locally still presents significant technical challenges.

For investors, the debate raises a question about Anthropic's future. Can the company generate enough demand for Claude to justify decades of infrastructure spending, or will cheaper alternatives eventually change the economics of AI?

Anthropic just became one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies. But does its enormous valuation mean Claude is better than ChatGPT?

The answer depends on what you're asking AI to do. Claude has built a strong reputation among developers, particularly through Claude Code, which can help write, debug and work with code across software projects.

It's also a popular choice for writing, analyzing documents and working through complex problems.

ChatGPT, meanwhile, offers an extensive collection of consumer-facing features, including image generation, voice conversations, research tools and coding capabilities through Codex.

Both companies are continually releasing new models and features, making it difficult to declare one chatbot the overall winner.

And Anthropic's IPO valuation isn't a measurement of Claude's intelligence. But it does reflect what investors are willing to pay for a stake in the business and their expectations about its future growth.

Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT or Claude, many people use these tools interchangeably, so the question isn't which one is better, but how can I best use each one.

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO is a major moment for the AI industry, but it also raises a question that has nothing to do with the stock market. If AI is becoming so powerful, what does this mean for the future of work?

The company behind Claude is developing technology that can already write code, analyze documents, conduct research and complete tasks that previously required human employees. And Anthropic's own research offers an interesting glimpse into how that could change the workplace.

In a recent study of its employees, the company found that coding-focused AI agent sessions among nontechnical workers increased dramatically, from two per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

The research also found signs of slowing junior employment in roles that use Claude for particularly complex tasks, although that doesn't establish that AI caused the slowdown.

Anthropic's IPO gives the company additional resources to expand its models and workplace tools. For employees, that could mean more opportunities to automate repetitive work, but it also raises concerns about which tasks companies will continue paying people to perform.

As we know, AI has already entered the workplace, so for now, it's about how quickly businesses adopt these tools and whether workers benefit from the productivity gains.

Anthropic just became a $2 trillion company, but does that mean Claude users should expect to pay more? Not necessarily.

For now, Anthropic's IPO doesn't automatically change the price of a Claude subscription.

Claude still offers a free version, while its Pro subscription costs $20 per month, or about $17 per month with annual billing. The company also offers higher-priced plans for people who need more extensive access to its AI models.

However, running powerful AI systems is expensive. Every conversation, coding session and complex research task requires computing resources.

As a public company, Anthropic will face greater scrutiny over its revenue, expenses and ability to become sustainably profitable.

That could influence future decisions about subscriptions, usage limits and premium features, although there's no evidence that the IPO itself will trigger an immediate price increase.

What might happen, is competitors might offer more, for less. ChatGPT already offers unlimited chatting, but we might see more Pro options among the free tier. This is something to watch for from Anthropic's biggest competitors.

Anthropic's historic IPO is attracting enormous excitement from investors, but buried in the company's financial disclosures is a warning about the technology making it so valuable.

Advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic warned in its IPO filing.

It's a striking admission from a company seeking billions of dollars from investors to develop increasingly powerful AI systems.

Anthropic has long positioned itself as a company focused on AI safety. Its founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, previously worked at OpenAI before launching their own AI research company in 2021.

But even Anthropic acknowledges that testing advanced AI models has limitations. In its IPO prospectus, the company warned that AI systems could develop unexpected capabilities during training, and that some potential dangers might not become apparent until after deployment.

These aren't predictions that an AI disaster is inevitable, but they are risks the company believes investors need to understand. For users like you and me, the warning highlights the challenges facing AI developers as chatbots become more capable than ever of taking actions, writing software and handling sensitive information.

Anthropic's IPO is a financial milestone, but its safety disclosures are a reminder that the technology's long-term consequences remain uncertain.OpenAI said they waited to file IPO for safety reasons.

Claude might be best known as a ChatGPT competitor, but Anthropic's biggest opportunity may be inside the workplace.

According to the company's IPO prospectus, more than half of Fortune 500 companies were Anthropic customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, 2026.

Anthropic also reported more than 1,900 customers generating at least $1 million in revenue over the same period, along with approximately 250 generating $10 million or more.

Those numbers offer a glimpse into why investors are willing to value the company so highly.

Businesses are using Claude for everything from software development to document analysis, insurance underwriting and cybersecurity. Unlike a consumer paying $20 per month for Claude Pro, large organizations can spend millions annually as they expand their use of AI.

Anthropic's success with Claude Code has also helped it establish a strong foothold among developers.

For everyday users, this is important because the next generation of Claude features may focus more on work rather than casual conversations like a typical chatbot.

#3234. ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Epilogue Scene Explained: How Everything Ties Together

SPOILER ALERT: This post spoils the end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

The epilogue scene at the end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping echoes the chapter that closes Suzanne Collins’ novel of the same name.

Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson appear in the final moment of the film, reprising their roles of Haymitch Abernathy, Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark, respectively, from The Hunger Games (2012), The Hunger Games: Catching Fire (2013), The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 (2014) and The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2 (2015).

It was known that Lawrence and Hutcherson would return for the second prequel film. Harrelson could have been a given once they were confirmed, since his character centers the latest movie. In The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which tells the villain origin story of Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth), Donald Sutherland’s voice was used in the end to tie the first prequel film to the original four, in which Sutherland portrayed the poisonous president. Watch on Deadline

The Sunrise scene in particular is meaningful with these three actors behind their roles because it connects the past and present, bridging the gap between The Sunrise on the Reaping and Suzanne Collins’ original trilogy of books plus their film adaptations. Haymitch, in his Quarter Quell Hunger Games, did so much to advance the rebellion that would eventually bring down Panem, the Capitol and the barbaric tradition that killed children ever year. It was Katniss who ultimately gained the momentum from this spark — symbolized by Haymitch’s flint striker and more — to topple the dystopian society and cruel reign of President Snow (Ralph Fiennes in Sunrise on the Reaping and Donald Sutherland in the first four films).

Katniss and Peeta wish Haymitch a happy birthday in the ending scene, symbolizing that he did, in fact, reach a birthday where the sun didn’t rise on another reaping ceremony, which was his love Lenore Dove’s (Whitney Peak) dying wish. It took another 25 years after his games, which doubled the amount of tributes entered as is custom for a Quarter Quell, to overcome the tyranny. The 50th Hunger Games added a wrinkle, or extra rule, to make those games extra gruesome.

By then, Peeta and Katniss, who had already somewhat thwarted the Gamemakers by threatening to each eat poisonous nightlock berries and die for there to be no victor in their 74th games, experienced a terrible Quarter Quell of their own. The 75th Hunger Games — or third Quarter Quell — involved the wrinkle that each pair of district tributes would be reaped from their existing pool of victors.

The Catching Fire film made it seem like Plutarch Heavensbee (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and President Snow (Donald Sutherland) devised that wrinkle themselves to particularly torture Katniss and send her a message about her sedition. In the books, the founders of Panem left a box behind that laid out the rules of each Quarter Quell game, making it seem more like coincidence that this happened when a full-blown rebellion was close at hand.

While preparing for the third Quarter Quell, Katniss and Peeta leaned on Haymitch for his experience in the games in addition to meeting other victors turned mentors turned tributes once more like Mags (Lynn Cohen), Beetee (Jeffrey Wright), Wiress (Amanda Plummer) and others, younger versions of whom played roles in Haymitch’s story before the big Catching Fire revolt as well.

“The seeds of Haymitch Abernathy’s backstory were planted over twenty years ago when I began the original trilogy,” author Suzanne Collins wrote in a letter timed to the film’s release. “In Catching Fire, Katniss and Peeta watch the recap of his Second Quarter Quell games as he silently observes from the shadows. The Capitol had warped the true account and spun reality into vicious propaganda. For Haymitch to tell the truth about what happened would’ve been too dangerous for his tributes and too traumatic for him.”

At the end of the snippet, Haymitch goes to the meadow to feed his flock of geese, which he raises in memory of Lenore Dove, but not before Katniss and Peeta thank him, and he in return thanks them for their teamwork in dismantling the dictatorship they lived under for so long.

As for whether there could be more films in the franchise, it seems like it would come down to Collins and her decision to write another book or two. Fans have been particularly vocal about wanting more of one Finnick Odair’s first Hunger Games, and director Francis Lawrence as well as star Joseph Zada have expressed interest in diving into Plutarch’s (Jesse Plemons) story as well as the lore behind the mysterious District 13, which makes itself known in the Mockingjay books and films. Collins is known for writing these books only when she has something to say and express through them. The final scene at the end of Sunrise on the Reaping could make a great close to the story as is.

#3232. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3228. Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI, including bank balances

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user …

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”

Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

#3227. Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at Age 65

Turning 65 unlocks Medicare, but it doesn't mean your Social Security check has reached its full size yet.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:00PM EST

For many workers, age 65 represents the first major gateway to retirement because it's when you become eligible for Medicare. While your health coverage begins at this milestone, your Social Security benefit might not be at its full strength. As of December 2025 -- the most recent data available -- the average benefit for 65-year-old retirees is $1,607.27 per month, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA).

This monthly average serves as a baseline for those eyeing the Medicare milestone. But if your full retirement age is 67, claiming at 65 means accepting a permanent 13.33% reduction in your monthly check. This reduction occurs because you're receiving payments for two additional years compared with those who wait until their full retirement age.

The average benefit varies significantly depending on work history and lifetime earnings. Among 65-year-olds, men receive an average of $1,772.00 per month. Women of the same age receive an average of $1,457.40, according to SSA data. This represents a monthly gap of $314.60 between the two groups.

These figures represent the average for all retirees who are currently age 65, regardless of when they first claimed their benefits. It's a snapshot of current payments rather than a projection of what any individual worker will receive. Your personal benefit depends on your specific earnings history and the exact month you choose to file.

Medicare eligibility at 65 doesn't mean you've reached full retirement age for Social Security. For everyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67. If you claim at 65, the SSA calculates your benefit by taking your average monthly income over your 35 highest-earning years, adjusting earlier wages for inflation, running it through the benefit formula, and then applying a permanent reduction for claiming early.

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027 to help benefits keep pace with inflation. This adjustment adds about $58 per month to the $1,607.27 average for 65-year-olds. Because the SSA designed these adjustments to protect purchasing power, they don't necessarily increase your standard of living; they simply aim to cover rising costs.

It's also important to frame Social Security as supplemental income. The program was designed to replace only about 40% of your pre-retirement income. Most retirees need a much higher share of their former earnings to maintain their lifestyle, so they generally rely on savings or other income sources to bridge the gap.

The claiming decision at 65 is often a trade-off between starting your benefits alongside Medicare or waiting for a higher monthly amount. If you live an average lifespan, you tend to receive roughly the same total regardless of when you claim. Comparing these averages to your own estimated benefit can help you decide if age 65 is the right time to file.

Every month that you delay your Social Security application increases your checks. From ages 65 to your FRA, your checks will grow by 5/9 of 1% per month, or about 6.67% per year.

Once you reach your FRA, your checks grow by 2/3 of 1% per month, or 8.00% per year, until you qualify for your largest benefit at age 70. Waiting beyond this point will only cost you money.

If you choose to delay your Social Security claim until you qualify for larger checks, don't make the mistake of delaying your Medicare application as well. Doing so could lead to lifetime premium increases that could make your retirement budget even tighter. Sign up for Medicare as soon as you can, and then choose the Social Security claiming age that makes the most sense to you.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.

#3226. Canva introduces new controls to hide generative AI features

In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today announced new controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:

The company says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything new. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the company’s design content library, Canva said that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

#3225. OLED iMac plans may be cancelled by Apple for two reasons

Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited …

1. The size. 24” is undesirable at the prices they ask.

2. No target display mode. Making the display unusable with multiple computers or after you’ve upgraded to a new model of Mac.

Adding OLED doesn’t solve either of these, and raising the price obviously doesn’t solve it.

At the same time, there’s an important distinction between commercial viability and margins. Apple is concerned with the latter, not the former.

An OLED iMac would be a commercially viable product at current prices, but it might not have the 30 to 40 % hardware profit margins they desire. Adding OLED would raise Apples costs, without adding more sales (due to 1 and 2) to offset that slightly lower but (still industry leading) profit margin.

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The company is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […]

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision.

For long-term investors, shifting 108 restaurants to franchise operators reduces capital requirements while securing a lower-cost, five-year debt structure. #3220. UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue …

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

This would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve said many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP …

The UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal said. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it launched – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

This ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

#3216. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3215. Why Helmerich & Payne Sank Today

The oil and gas equipment vendor saw headwinds due to the war in Saudi Arabia.

By Billy Duberstein – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:04PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Helmerich & Payne ›

Shares of oil and gas equipment vendor Helmerich & Payne (HP -7.71%) fell 7.7% on Thursday.

HP delivered its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings report today. While adjusted earnings results beat expectations, the conflict in the Middle East led to a big impairment charge, with management noting subdued activity there that should continue through 2027.

In the third quarter, HP's revenue grew roughly 8% to $1.09 billion, while adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings per share rose to $0.36, up from a slight loss in the year-ago quarter. Both figures beat analyst expectations.

However, HP's GAAP bottom line fell into a large loss, as the company took a $610 million impairment charge on assets in the Middle East. It appears management deems some of its equipment in the region either damaged or unprofitable to maintain due to the war in Iran and the related conflict between the Houthis of Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

Going forward, management noted recent suspensions of conventional drilling activity in Saudi Arabia, and projected fewer active rigs in the country next quarter, with "the potential for further activity reductions over the course of the year."

Even amid geopolitical turmoil, the broader market was down today, possibly due to fears of further interest rate hikes. The Federal Reserve's minutes show officials remain concerned about inflation, which oil and gas product prices have driven to a large extent. Higher interest rates could slow growth or potentially cause a recession, which may hurt oil and gas demand going forward, even as the Middle East conflict threatens supply.

Ultimately, Helmerich & Payne’s stock looks cheap after today's decline, with roughly a $5 billion enterprise value and trailing adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) of $913 million, implying a 5.5 multiple. However, that cheap valuation is due to the cyclical and unpredictable nature of global conventional energy investment, which is highly volatile, as this year has shown.

#3214. Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.
