#3212. Model ML raises $250m at a $1.5bn valuation for bankers’ AI agents

Model ML’s annual recurring revenue grew 12 times in a year. Its CEO says the startup’s AI agents now help banks earn money, and are no longer just tools that save time.

Model ML co-founders Chaz and Arnie Englander in London.

Model ML, a London startup that builds AI agents for bankers, consultants and investors, has raised $250m at a $1.5bn valuation. General Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the Series B round, the company said on Tuesday.

Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The round takes Model ML’s total funding to $350m. FT Partners led its $75m Series A in November 2025, and HSBC Asset Management invested in August.

In the third quarter, Model ML’s annual recurring revenue grew 12 times year on year and its daily active users rose 26 times, the company said. It will use the money to grow its research and engineering teams in London and New York.

Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander founded Model ML in 2023, Bloomberg reported. They previously co-founded Fat Llama, a rental marketplace that Sweden’s Hygglo bought for $41.5m in 2022, TechCrunch reported.

Each user gets an agent that runs on the firm’s own systems and data. When news breaks on a company a banker covers, the agent judges whether it matters and prepares the analysis in the firm’s formats. It works in tools such as Excel and PowerPoint to build pitch decks and due diligence reports.

“AI should do more than give you another answer or notification. It should understand your work and get things done,” said Chaz Englander, Model ML’s co-founder and CEO.

Model ML sends each task to the AI model that suits it best. A growing share runs on its own fine-tuned open-source models. On the work they handle, these cost 2% as much as frontier models and are in most cases five times faster, the company said. It added that customer data is never used to train AI models.

Banks have tied job cuts to AI. Barclays said in October it would cut 5,000 jobs, and Standard Chartered plans to cut 7,800 jobs in back-office roles by 2030. Englander played down the idea that Model ML is mainly a way to cut costs.

“The average age of a Model ML user is 33 years old, not 23 years old,” Englander told Bloomberg. “These tools are no longer productivity and efficiency tools. They’re revenue generative.”

Revenue is split fairly evenly across banks, consulting firms and asset managers, he said. Model ML’s rivals include New York’s Rogo, which raised $160m at a $2bn valuation in April. OpenAI and Anthropic also sell AI tools to financial professionals.

#3211. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

#3209. NJ Resources (NJR) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Bill cuts and a raised clean energy target shape the new fiscal outlook.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:10PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

New Jersey Resources (NJR -3.46%) reported fiscal 2026 net financial earnings of $3.58 per share and initiated its fiscal 2027 guidance range of $3.25 to $3.40 per share. Management reported a sixth consecutive year of exceeding initial guidance and a 31st consecutive year of dividend increases. The company updated its five-year capital plan to a range of $5.3 billion to $5.7 billion, with more than 60% of investments focused on safety and reliability at New Jersey Natural Gas. Strategic priorities for fiscal 2027 include managing customer affordability through bill reductions and expanding storage capacity at the Leaf River facility to meet growing demand in the PJM market.

Operator: Hello, and thank you for standing by. My name is Trevor, and I will be your conference operator today. I would like to welcome everyone to the New Jersey Resources Fiscal 2026 Fourth Quarter and Year-End Financial Results Conference Call. All lines have been placed on mute to prevent any background noise. After the speaker's remarks, there will be a question-and-answer session for members of the financial community. To ask a question, press star one. To withdraw your question, press star one again. As a reminder, today's conference is being recorded and will be available for replay on New Jersey Resources Investor Relations website at investor.njresources.com. I would now like to turn the call over to Karin Daly.

Karin Daly: Thank you, Trevor, and good morning. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that certain statements in today's call may contain estimates and other forward-looking statements. The current expectations, assumptions, and beliefs forming the basis of our forward-looking statements include many factors that are beyond our ability to control or estimate precisely. This could cause results to materially differ from our expectations, as found on slide two. These items can also be found in our forward-looking statements section of yesterday's earnings release and in our most recent forms 10-K and 10-Q, as filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

We do not assume any obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements referenced herein in light of future events. We will also be referring to certain non-GAAP financial measures, such as net financial earnings, or NFE. We believe that NFE, net financial loss, utility gross margin, financial margin, adjusted funds from operations, and adjusted debt provide a more complete understanding of our financial performance. However, these non-GAAP measures are not intended to be a substitute for GAAP. Our non-GAAP financial measures are discussed more fully in item seven of our 10-K. Today's presentation and the most recent earnings press release were furnished with yesterday's form 8-K and are available on our website.

I am joined by Stephen Westhoven, President and Chief Executive Officer, Roberto Bel, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, as well as other members of our senior management team. Stephen will begin with an overview of our fiscal 2026 performance and fiscal 2027 outlook, followed by a review of our business units. Roberto will then review detailed fiscal 2026 financial results, introduce our fiscal 2027 guidance and capital plan, and discuss our current financial position. Stephen will then return with closing remarks before we open the call for questions. I'll now turn the call over to Stephen.

Stephen Westhoven: Thanks, Karin, and good morning, everyone. Before I begin, I would like to take a moment to formally welcome Karin Daly, who joined NJR this week as our Head of Investor Relations. We are excited to have her on board and know she is also looking forward to working with all of you. With that, let us get started with our fiscal 2026 performance. New Jersey Resources delivered net financial earnings of $3.58 per share, our sixth consecutive year exceeding our initial guidance. We also raised our dividend for the 31st consecutive year. This performance reflects the strength of our complementary businesses and the ability of our employees to execute.

Across the entire company, our team delivered exceptional service through periods of extreme weather and record system throughput. We prioritized affordability for our customers while continuing to make critical investments in safety and reliability of our infrastructure. Here are some of the highlights from each business unit. At New Jersey Natural Gas, we remain focused on the fundamentals of safety, reliability, and affordability. Ahead of the winter heating season, we have lowered the average residential customer bill by 9% while continuing to invest in our system, add customers, and advance our base rate case. Clean Energy Ventures added 72.4 MW of new capacity through the completion of 14 solar projects.

At the same time, the team continued to advance its strong pipeline of investment options that will drive growth over the coming years. Storage and Transportation grew revenue through re-contracting and made significant progress on its growth strategy by securing its FERC certificate for the expansion at Leaf River. Energy Services generated significant cash flows that were reinvested in our infrastructure businesses, reducing our need for new debt. Home Services helped keep customers' homes comfortable through this year's extreme weather and was named Ruud's Top 20 Pro Partner for the 10th consecutive year. Now turning to our outlook on slide six.

Today, we are initiating fiscal 2027 NFEPS guidance in the range of $3.25-$3.40 per share, consistent with our long-term growth target of 7%-9%. We are also updating our five-year capital plan through fiscal 2031 at a range of $5.3 billion-$5.7 billion. More than 60% of this capital is planned for our regulated utility, with a focus on safety, reliability, and energy efficiency. Importantly, we expect to fund this plan without block equity while maintaining strong credit metrics. Roberto will provide more detail on the capital and financing plan later in the presentation. Turning to slide seven, our outlook is built around key strategic priorities: customer affordability, consistent execution, disciplined capital deployment, and robust organic growth across our infrastructure businesses.

At New Jersey Natural Gas, we expect continued rate base growth through fiscal 2031, driven by customer additions, investments in safety and reliability, and energy efficiency programs that provide customers cost savings opportunities. At Storage and Transportation, we expect net financial earnings to double from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2027, driven by favorable re-contracting at both Leaf River and Adelphia. In addition, the phase 1 of Leaf River expansion is fully contracted and now under construction. At Clean Energy Ventures, we expect to grow our installed capacity significantly, helping to meet the need for new electric supply in the markets we serve.

CEV is well-positioned with a robust pipeline of ITC-eligible projects and organic growth opportunities that capitalize on our existing assets. I'll walk through each business, starting with New Jersey Natural Gas on slide eight. Managing cost impacts for our customers remains central to how we run New Jersey Natural Gas. Natural gas remains by far the most cost-effective way for our customers to heat their homes and businesses. Throughout fiscal 2026, we took several steps to strengthen this value proposition. New Jersey Natural Gas's customer bill reduction of 9% went into effect on October 1st. That translates to an annual savings of over $150 for the average residential customer.

We invested a record $101 million through SAVEGREEN, helping customers reduce energy use and lower their bills by up to 30%. We also prioritized assistance for our most vulnerable customers. This year, we hosted 27 energy assistance days throughout our service territory. These are dedicated in-person outreach events to enroll customers in energy assistance and bill payment programs. Through these efforts, New Jersey Natural Gas helped connect our most in-need customers with nearly $21 million in bill payment assistance. That's money that stays with families across our service territory. Turning to slide nine, earlier this year, the company made a coordinated set of regulatory filings with the objective of mitigating customer bill impacts while recovering our investments.

The initial filings provided for a 9% bill reduction, as previously mentioned. We also filed for a base rate increase to recover investments in safety and reliability. The rate case is moving forward as expected, with a resolution anticipated by the end of the winter heating season. We expect that the impact of their base rate case, combined with the recently implemented bill reduction, will leave customer bills nearly flat compared to where they were at the time of the filings. On the customer growth side, the utility continues to see steady customer additions from a mix of conversions and new construction.

In fiscal 2027, we expect to reach 600,000 customers served, a milestone achievement for the company, reflecting the execution and commitment of our employees every day. Turning to S&T on slide 10, over the last decade, total U.S. natural gas demand, including exports, increased 45%, but working storage capacity remained nearly unchanged. That imbalance reinforces the value of flexible, strategically located storage. This has created opportunities at Leaf River for both favorable re-contracting and organic expansion. We are moving rapidly to execute on these opportunities. As mentioned earlier, phase one of our Leaf River expansion is fully contracted, and we initiated construction in October. We expect the incremental 5.1 BCF of working capacity to be brought into service in 2028.

In total, our FERC authorization allows for the expansion of Leaf River's capacity to more than 55 BCF. Looking ahead, Leaf River has even more capacity to grow, including the potential for additional caverns. Successful re-contracting is expected to double S&T's NFE between fiscal years 2025 and 2027 to a range of $37 million-$42 million. This updated range, slightly lower than previously communicated, reflects the short-term reduction in operational flexibility during construction of phase one of Leaf River. By fiscal 2029, the short-term capital cost impact will be resolved, and S&T NFE is poised to grow in the range of $55 million-$65 million.

Turning to Clean Energy Ventures on slide 11, our proactive approach to safe harboring provides a strategic advantage that will drive significant solar capital deployment into fiscal 2030. CEV's project pipeline is unique. We have secured investment options, largely through joint development agreements that provide CEV with the right, but not the obligation, to invest. This optionality gives us flexibility to direct capital opportunistically. CEV is also pursuing additional opportunities that leverage the long-term value of our grid-connected solar assets. We see a real opportunity to optimize our already built and paid-for solar interconnections through the use of battery storage and other distributed generation, such as fuel cells and linear generators.

Importantly, as part of the Big Beautiful Bill, these technologies will continue to benefit from investment tax credits into the 2030s. A strong example of this strategy is our recent acquisition of two Massachusetts solar plus storage projects, both of which are now under construction. These projects both pair 15 MW of solar arrays with 9 MW of on-site batteries. This allows for the interconnection to be used for more hours of the day and for generation to be shifted into peak demand hours, with the goal of lowering prices. Given our objective to invest in solar firming technologies, we are transitioning our discussion of in-service capital and project pipeline from megawatts in service to capital expenditure in service.

We believe that these types of investments are not appropriately captured by a megawatt-based installed capacity metric. In the 16 years we've operated CEV, we've established best-in-class capabilities around developing, building, and operating distributed generation assets. One thing is clear: distributed generation plays a vital role in today's energy landscape, and its importance will only continue to grow in the years ahead. With that, I'll turn the call over to Roberto for the financial review and outlook. Roberto?

Roberto Bel: Thanks, Stephen. Good morning, everyone. Fiscal 2026 reflected solid execution across New Jersey Resources' complementary businesses. Consolidated NFE was $361.7 million, or $3.58 per share. We raised NFEPS guidance by $0.45 during the year and exceeded initial guidance for a sixth consecutive year. In terms of segment contributions, New Jersey Natural Gas represented approximately 60% of consolidated NFE. Turning to capital investment on slide 14, we invested $833 million in fiscal 2026 across our infrastructure businesses. New Jersey Natural Gas invested approximately $600 million, including SAVEGREEN. About 40% of that earned near real-time returns. Clean Energy Ventures invested approximately $170 million, primarily focused on developing, constructing, and acquiring commercial-scale solar energy facilities.

Storage and Transportation invested approximately $63 million and advanced the expansion of existing caverns at Leaf River. Moving to slide 15, we're initiating fiscal 2027 NFEPS guidance in the range of $3.25-$3.40, consistent with our 7%-9% long-term annual growth target. We expect New Jersey Natural Gas to contribute 60%-65% of fiscal 2027 NFE. Clean Energy Ventures is expected to contribute 14%-18%, Storage and Transportation 10%-14%, and Energy Services 8%-14%. Our strong NFEPS projections are supported by a robust capital plan, as reflected on slide 16. From fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2031, we plan to invest in the range of $5.3 billion-$5.7 billion, with over 60% of those investments dedicated to New Jersey Natural Gas.

For the next two years, through fiscal 2028, we expect capital investment to reach approximately $2.3 billion, with roughly $1.1 billion invested in fiscal 2027. Clean Energy Ventures will represent a significant portion of the capital deployed at our unregulated subsidiaries, as solar and battery storage are among the most efficient ways to bring new supply to the grid. Our Clean Energy segment is uniquely positioned to address increasing market demand. As such, we are raising our 2027 expected capital expenditure target for Clean Energy Ventures to a range of $400 million-$500 million, up from $270 million-$370 million. Turning to slide 17, our financing plan is designed to fund our strategic growth well within our credit capacity.

For fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2031, projected sources and uses are approximately $6.7 billion. The plan includes about $5.5 billion of investment and $1.2 billion of dividends, funded primarily by approximately $3.9 billion of operating cash flow and $2.6 billion of debt, with a very modest amount of equity. Our adjusted FFO to adjusted debt ratio was 25% in fiscal 2026, aided by very strong cash generation at Energy Services. We expect this metric to average 20%-21% over the next five years, providing financial flexibility as we execute a significant organic investment program. Finally, on slide 18, our balance sheet and liquidity support the capital plan.

As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately $2.9 billion of notes and first mortgage bonds. The maturity schedule is well laddered, with no significant concentration in any one year. We have $900 million of committed credit facilities available through fiscal 2031. Our secured utility ratings remain strong and unchanged, A1 at Moody's and A+ at Fitch, both with stable outlooks that were reaffirmed earlier this year. Based on our current plan and given our financial strength to fund capital expenditures, we do not anticipate a need to issue any block equity over the next five years. I will now turn the call back to Stephen.

Stephen Westhoven: Thanks, Roberto. I will close where I started, with our customers. Everything in our plan begins with delivering affordable, safe, reliable energy to the families and businesses we serve. at New Jersey Natural Gas, our growing customer base, the cost advantage of natural gas, and our service excellence are the core of how we operate. All of our other businesses complement that foundation. Clean Energy Ventures is set to deploy significant capital on new and organic projects that help meet the pressing need for more electric supply. Storage and Transportation is set for robust growth in the coming years, providing storage and pipeline capacity that supports reliable supply backed by long-term contracts.

Energy Services generates additional cash flows that contribute to earnings that can be reinvested in our businesses. Our priorities remain clear: keep energy affordable, operate safely and reliably, deploy capital in a disciplined manner, and grow where NJR has a strategic advantage. Finally, I want to thank our employees across NJR. Your dedication to our customers is what drives everything we do. With that, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star one again. We ask that you pick up your handset when asking a question to allow for optimum sound quality. If you are muted locally, please remember to unmute your device. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Your first question comes from the line of Gabe Moreen with Mizuho. Gabe, your line is open.

Gabe Moreen: Good morning, team. Maybe if I can start out on CEV and the boosted outlook there. Can you just talk about, and it seems like it's not just for 2027, it's for 2028 as well, in terms of this boosted level of CapEx and growth, hopefully. Can you talk about the degree to which all of that is contracted at this point? Your confidence in terms of any permits you might need to secure that CapEx spend, and relatedly, the mention of the 350 MW of interconnects in PJM. Does any of that CapEx capture some of that opportunity, or is that going to be something potentially separate from this elevated CapEx or higher CapEx?

Stephen Westhoven: Hey, Gabe. Thanks for the question. We put that in the capital plan, so obviously we've got a high degree of confidence that we're going to be able to execute. A number of factors are basically making that CapEx plan what it is. Certainly, support policies pushing this forward, distributed gen has been popular, speed to market capability, and also returns have been attractive. So, in a diversified company like ours, we're able to put capital where you have attractive returns and shift, and that's what you see in that capital plan that you have going forward.

Gabe Moreen: Okay, great. As far as the interconnects and the like, sorry, Stephen, I don't know if I caught an answer. Is that embedded to a degree in that capital plan, taking advantage of those?

Stephen Westhoven: You'll have to The interconnects, are you talking about the interconnect process, or are you talking about the-

Gabe Moreen: Oh, I just mean like the cited in the slide, the 350 MW that you've got potentially at your existing sites to interconnect more power into the grid.

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah, I think in the early years, we're working, or we're, for the solar that we're making investments in, not so much taking advantage of those interconnects at this point. That would take place in your outer years, where we'd be able to expand and take advantage of those. And that would be part of that solar firming strategy that we talk about.

Gabe Moreen: Got it. Okay, thanks, Stephen. And then maybe if I can just follow up in terms of the program year seven request in terms of vis-à-vis the SAVEGREEN program. Can you talk about kind of the two options you're proposing at the BPU, and to what extent you're assuming that those move forward in your guidance and capital at this point?

Patrick Migliaccio: Yeah, I think, good morning, Gabe. It's technically actually. So encouraged because the new administration affirmed its commitment to energy efficiency, which, as everyone knows, is one of the most effective ways that we have to reduce customer bills. The extension will take us one more program year through June of 2028, and gives us a runway for just the EE programs with a path to achieve the historical ROEs. And so, we're in the process where we submitted proposals, which is an important step for having active dialogue with the Board of Public Utilities, and expect resolution sometime in spring of 2027.

Gabe Moreen: Great. Thanks, Patrick. Appreciate it.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Eli Jossen with JPMorgan. Eli, your line is open.

Eli Jossen: Hey, good morning, everybody. Thanks for taking the questions. Just wanted to start on the CapEx plan shaping through the period. Hey, just obviously you have stronger 2027 and 2028 figures, but if we think about the back half of the plan and what might drive upside, and how you're risk-weighting certain opportunities. But yeah, just broadly the shaping of the plan and thinking about the trajectory that you've given today. Thanks.

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah, Eli, diversified company, we've got a number of options to be able to deploy capital. You see that, as I said before to Gabe, we were able to shift the plan to where most attractive returns are. Options going forward for us, certainly utility will be a big driver of our CapEx, energy efficiency, like Patrick just talked about. CEV has a lot of optionality, especially in the back half of the plan with all those interconnects that are already existing that we could take advantage of, speed to market being very important there, and the capacity markets of PJM. Leaf River, we've got our first phase that we started.

We sort of put a little bit of capital to work in doing the groundwork to decide on our second phase expansion of Leaf River. There's even expansions beyond that. We haven't talked about the Adelphia Gateway pipeline that does have some expansion as well. When you look at the plan that we have along with the diversified businesses that we have, a lot of options to be able to expand going forward. Given the macro push and growth in the energy markets, we feel like we're really well-positioned to take advantage of that.

Eli Jossen: Awesome. Then maybe just shifting to the EPS CAGR. I know you guys are in the middle of a rate case and are constantly reassessing the outlook, but can you remind us how we should think about your overall rebasing strategy and what you might need to see to think about rebasing at your next roll forward? And yeah, just the rebasing strategy overall. Thanks.

Roberto Bel: Hey, Eli. This is Roberto. So if you look at us historically, we've been rebasing every two to three years. So most likely, we'll be rebasing next year. But having said that, just remember that the way we measure our growth projections is based on our 2025 initial guidance, removing the gain from the solar sale, of the residential solar sale. And just to remind everyone, what we have been doing over a number of years now, about six years, is we have been increasing our guidance every year at a midpoint of about 8% or so. So it's been a very modest increase in guidance. So hopefully that gives you some context.

And how is the $2.1 billion CEV pipeline reflected within that timeframe?

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah. We expect that moving forward, 60% of our capital, 60% of our earnings majority is still coming from the utility, and we have that through the five-year plan. You might see some slight shifts, but we don't expect anything to disrupt those metrics as we say them.

Constantine Lednev: Okay. Understood. And the $2.1 billion, just in terms of the timing of how that's reflected within the five-year, is that fully incorporated or partially?

Stephen Westhoven: I think there'll be some variability to it, obviously, just through construction schedules and things like that, just as a practical execution. But we expect to have it as a steady line with a little bit of growth that's associated with it and oriented to growth metrics of the company.

Constantine Lednev: Okay. Understood. Maybe just shifting to New Jersey, just with the few different regulatory approaches that we've seen on rate cases in the current cycle, any thoughts on how competitive the case is relative to the EO1 kind of mandates and any read-throughs from other ongoing cases, like the use of deferral accounting and such?

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah. As far as the EO1 goes, it's mainly concentrated on the electrics. For our rate case, it's been just a regular rate case. There's nothing in there that's out of the ordinary, and we've been proceeding forward like we have in the past. So it's being processed as normal. That is really the only thing I can tell you about it.

Constantine Lednev: Okay. Just on the business review process, any read-throughs, any positive read-throughs from the proposals that were out there? There's some talk of multi-year constructs and performance mechanisms.

Constantine Lednev: Okay. Understood. Appreciate the time today. Thanks.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Julien Dumoulin-Smith with Jefferies. Julien, your line is open.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Hey. Good morning, team. How you guys all doing? Nice to chat.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Hey. Thanks again for the time. Look, just a couple cleanup items at this point. Just following up a little bit on the tone from some of the earlier questions. How do you think about just rate base growth? I think you guys pulled that from the deck versus last time. It might be more of a technicality, but how do you think about that through 2030 here and just any twists or turns about that? Then how do you think about rate base growth given the fact that you guys have CapEx through 2031 at this point? Just, I know there's a little bit of different years in the deck.

Stephen Westhoven: I mean, rate base growth has been really regular. We've got a pipeline of investments at the utility that really follow the same year on year on year. Customer growth is robust. We've got vintage pipeline that needs to be replaced, and we've got that program that we continue to move forward. You can see the breakdown as we break down our capital plan. Energy efficiency, a big part of it, and with the concentration on affordability, we expect that to maintain. Patrick had referenced that earlier when he was talking about energy efficiency. So really, it's kind of the same old story with the utility. We're in a good place.

Natural gas is the cheapest way that you can heat your home or business and maintaining reliability, being sensitive to our customers at the same time, and marrying those two things together, put together the rate base growth and the investments that we've got outlined here.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Got it. So no change to the 7%-9% from prior years?

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Okay, excellent. Then just coming back to the CEV side of things, just real quickly. I mean, obviously, seeing a little bit of an uptick here. You talk about a higher percentage from the last year, the 14%, 18% from 10%. How does that evolve through the plan here? Can you talk about that a little bit? What is driving that uptick in CEV this specific year? Is it tax credits, or how do you think about credit transfers, just the sale-leaseback?

Then ultimately, just given that you have given a 2031 CapEx number here, can you talk about the plan around CEV, specifically solar versus maybe some storage focus, as you think about the credit program evolution here in cliff, if you will? How do you think about the different programs that you could pivot into?

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah. I think, for your first part of your question, just kind of the earlier part of the CapEx plan, CEV team has done a great job basically of safe harboring a number of projects. You can see, as we have talked about, we have got a big pipeline, the ability to kind of move that forward or move that around based on returns. We are seeing attractive returns. So the result of those things and favorable policy environment, certainly a pull in the kind of the macro capacity market, needed capacity in PJM, all those things factor into tailwinds for CEV right now.

You can see that we have changed the metric from megawatts to CapEx, that we are anticipating slight shift going forward. This would be out in the later years. Distributed generation is really popular. You can see that with hyperscalers and things like that. We are seeing those trends moving forward, and we have the opportunity here with all of our existing interconnects to be able to leverage those and put capacity in the ground quickly. We are working towards that. We have got a confident plan. We have got good projects lined up for this foreseeable future, and that all factors into the CapEx plan that you see this morning.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: And maybe just ask explicitly, do you have a 2031 CEV kind of budget that you would kind of target us in on? And I know you guys are maybe less granular normally.

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah. We give the granularity in the prompt year and the next year, but we are giving the broad number for the outer years, and we will leave it at that. Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Yeah. No, I appreciate that perspective here. And then just a quick complement to that. Any particular points that you would flag as other notable offsets in the back half of the year, or back half of the plan? I apologize.

Stephen Westhoven: Yeah. You know what? We have We are an infrastructure company. We have a lot of existing infrastructure on the ground, and the easiest way to be able to meet growing demand in the marketplace is to use your existing infrastructure. So when we think about growth in the back half of the plan, all of our existing infrastructure is available for expansion. It is just a matter of being able to put together the right policies, permitting customers and things like that in order to meet the market. You can see this in a smaller way with Leaf River right now. It is existing asset, brownfield development.

It is the most economic to bring the market in a market that is short on storage. I think that theme carries through across our entire company and will continue to drive our growth in the outer years of the capital plan.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Excellent. Thank you guys very much. Best of luck. Nice to chat.

Stephen Westhoven: All right. Thanks, Julien. Thanks.

Operator: Your next question comes from Travis Miller with Morningstar. Travis, your line is open.

Travis Miller: Good morning, everyone. Thank you.

Travis Miller: SAVEGREEN, how much of that CapEx forecast for 2027 and 2028 depends on the outcome of the regulatory proposal?

Patrick Migliaccio: Travis, a very de minimis amount. We recall that the T2, which I think was a PY6 program, authorized about $380 million of investment. As you look forward in our capital plan, very little of what we have in that plan is tied to anything related to a program extension. That said, we're optimistic about the programs. As I mentioned earlier, it was one of the best tools that we had to help lower energy demand. Particularly when you think about the energy supply situation in Jersey, every megawatt saved, every dekatherm saved is only used for economic growth and development. We're optimistic that we'll continue through here.

Travis Miller: Okay. Yeah. Kind of along that thought process, how long could that runway of, call it $90 or so million of investment go? Is there some point at which energy efficiency meets a diminishing returns type of situation? Or how long do you see that kind of $90 million run rate going?

Patrick Migliaccio: Yeah. So the easiest way to think about that, Travis Miller, is that when we look at the programs that have been in place since 2009, we've had roughly 120,000 customers participate through that energy efficiency program, predominantly residential and some commercial. So from a market penetration perspective, we're only 20% of the way there on a 600,000 customer count. All that being said, not everyone would benefit from that type of message. So there's a fair bit of runway here. So long as the policy environment is supportive, we think there's market opportunity.

Travis Miller: Okay, great. Then shifting over to CEV, when you talk about distributed generation, putting capacity on the ground, can we read through that combined with your shift to the dollar amount versus megawatts that we're going to see some more battery investment and battery plus storage, possibly other types of-

Stephen Westhoven: You saw today, I'm sorry, Travis, you saw today, right? We announced the Massachusetts project. You mentioned that in the script. We've got some batteries that are already starting to be deployed, and we're making investments in. So, like I said, I think that and the ability to efficiently use our interconnects is going to create the scenario where you're going to be able to make investments where balancing and optimization are going to drive our ability to serve load and reduce capacity costs on the grid.

Travis Miller: Okay. And when you say interconnects, using interconnects, that means putting batteries there, not putting more solar panels there, right?

Stephen Westhoven: I was referring to our existing interconnects, the existing interconnects that we have on our grid-connected solar facilities.

Travis Miller: You could put batteries there, basically, right?

Stephen Westhoven: That is correct. That is right.

Stephen Westhoven: We are distributed generation.

Travis Miller: Okay. And one other real quick one. Are there any large single customers? You mentioned real briefly data centers, but are there any large single customers that you have contracted with that would be included in those CapEx figures?

Stephen Westhoven: I mean, there's always points when we're developing solar, and those are behind the meter, so they do have a customer associated with it, but nothing that's out of the normal or worth highlighting at this point.

Travis Miller: Okay, perfect. Appreciate all the thoughts.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Chris Ellinghaus with Siebert Williams Shank. Chris, your line is open.

Chris Ellinghaus: Hey, everybody. Good morning. Stephen, I think you kind of insinuated this when you referred to speed to market and the interconnect issue, but can you say, in your increased CapEx, are you seeing some improved return expectations also sort of motivating the increase in the CapEx numbers for CEV?

The CEV group did a great job, safe harboring projects, put ourselves in a position where we were able to really choose the best projects to make investments in. I think your statement there does line up. The returns are attractive, and that's one of the reasons that you see increased capital moving towards that in our plan.

Chris Ellinghaus: Okay, that's helpful. On slide 10, for S&T, you sort of referenced your ability to expand on your existing infrastructure and talked about caverns in Adelphia. Would it be fair to say that you still have some investment decisions for that 2031 bar that you haven't outlined in that green bar that lead you to that sort of undefined 2032 upside that you haven't made yet? What's still yet to go into those decisions to lead to some of those further expansions?

Stephen Westhoven: In that green bar, you've got a phase 2 expansion. That was all part of the FERC certificate that we received. There was like three parts of that FERC certificate. You had phase 1 expansion, cavern expansion, and phase 2 cavern expansion, and then there was also compression associated with it. We haven't made the decision for the final phase 2 expansion, but we have started investing capital in that place, but FID hasn't been made. That's all part of that green bar. Aside from all that, the Leaf River Energy Complex, large complex, a number of salt and storage capability fields for development are down in that area, and there is additional expansion in that field.

There's always the possibility to be able to expand beyond that 2031. Not covered in our FERC certificate, we haven't decided on that yet, but that organic growth is still there for us.

Chris Ellinghaus: Okay. Lastly, with the election results, has that influenced your thinking at all? Maybe not in the current CapEx numbers, but has it altered your sort of longer-term thinking and planning for CEV?

Stephen Westhoven: You know what? It hasn't. I mean, we're a business model, energy infrastructure, energy grows in the U.S. Administrations are going to come and go, but those macro drivers that grow the need for additional power and energy are going to be here and are going to continue. I really just see that we've got such great macro fundamentals that energy's going to continue to grow, and because we're existing infrastructure, we're going to participate in that.

Not just yet, but at some point in the future, we might. I mean, you kind of saw that shift that we have made, like I said, from megawatts to the CapEx. We are already starting to shift in that way. So, we will make changes to reflect the business and try to help people understand we are making investments and essentially the growth prospects for our company as we can.

Chris Ellinghaus: That might be helpful to sort of model expected returns to know what type of assets are in that bucket, maybe. Anyway, thanks. Appreciate the detail.

#3208. iPadOS 27.3: Three new features coming to your iPad

iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all users next month, here are three new features it introduces for iPad.

There’s a new setting in iPadOS 27.3 that I instantly turned on and have been loving. It lets you double-tap the top of a window to resize it.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if ‘Windowed Apps’ is enabled there’s now a new toggle: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom.’

I’ve been using this gesture all the time in the beta, because it lets me resize my window to fullscreen then revert it to its previous size with ease. It’s an intuitive, convenient way to resize windows for different tasks.

Read more: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

Visual intelligence was available on iPad already, but iPadOS 27.3 adds a dedicated hub for using the feature: a new Siri mode in the Camera app.

iOS 27 brought Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app, but it was missing from iPad. iPadOS 27.3 corrects that oversight, letting you use your iPad’s built-in Camera app to ask Siri about any object you capture.

Baking visual intelligence into Camera should expose the feature to a lot more iPad users, since before you had to set up a custom control or shortcut for it. And with how much better visual intelligence has gotten thanks to Siri AI, the Siri mode is a valuable addition.

Read more: iOS 27 gives the Camera app on iPhone a brand new mode

Freeform is gaining a variety of new features in iPadOS 27.3. They’re available in macOS and iOS too, but out of all Apple platforms, Freeform feels very much built for the iPad.

Which iPadOS 27.3 features are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

#3207. Google’s Gemini can now take over tasks on your Mac

Google's assistant works in a background window, but it can also delete or share files by mistake.

Google’s Gemini assistant can now take over tasks on a Mac, clicking through apps, typing and filling in forms for you. Google announced on Thursday that computer use is rolling out in the Gemini app for Mac.

You describe a task, and Gemini works through it across local files, desktop apps and websites. It runs in a separate background window with a live preview in the chat, so your screen and cursor stay free. You choose which apps it can use, can pause it, and must approve key actions.

Google’s examples include pulling weights and addresses from PDFs into a shipping quote form, and turning dashboard data into a Google Slides deck. It can also batch-edit photos or prepare resale listings from pictures in a folder.

Google warns that Gemini can make mistakes, including permanently deleting files or sharing them with others. It is designed to ask permission first, and it can only see folders you connect. Backups of changed files are deleted after 24 hours or when you start a new task.

Google is also building Gemini into the operating system of its Googlebook laptops, as rivals race to put agents on the desktop. OpenAI’s ChatGPT can log your keystrokes on a Mac to build its memory. Agents built on the OpenClaw framework have helped drive Mac mini demand.

#3205. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3203. Is Nvidia Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity After Its Latest Earnings?

There is a light at the end of the tunnel for Nvidia.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:15PM EST

The past week has been hard on Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%). The semiconductor leader had to separate from its co-founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang, after he was embroiled in a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Colette Kress, who remains CFO, has stepped up as interim CEO, leading the company through its first quarterly update since Huang's departure.

And what an update it was. Nvidia once again crushed expectations, but that wasn't enough to jolt the stock, which remains down significantly since it reached a new all-time high in early October. Is Nvidia a generational buying opportunity at current levels?

Death, taxes, and Nvidia's financial results coming in above analysts' projections seem to be the only certain things these days. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, the company's revenue came in at $115.8 billion, up 103% compared to the year-ago period. Data center revenue grew 110% year over year to $107.6 billion.

Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin was 74.9%, compared to the 73.5% reported in the prior-year quarter. The semiconductor specialist's non-GAAP operating income was $77.9 billion, rising 116% year over year, while its non-GAAP earnings per share were $2.68, up 111% year over year.

The fact that profits are growing faster than revenue is a strong sign for Nvidia, given the industry's increasing competitiveness. While some investors worry that competition from custom AI chips will erode the company's pricing power in the GPU (graphics processing unit) market, as hyperscalers and other corporations increasingly opt for these custom chips, it seems, at least, that this hasn't happened yet. Improving margins are a sign that Nvidia maintains strong pricing power.

Meanwhile, Nvidia's free cash flow for the period was $43.8 billion, rising 98% year over year. The company also posted excellent guidance. Nvidia expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) for its fourth quarter. That would represent a 91% year-over-year increase.

Of course, Nvidia's financial results and guidance were only part of the story. The market wants to know how the company's efforts to replace Huang are going. Nvidia said it isn't interested in bringing back Huang, despite many people, both inside and outside the company, calling for his reinstatement. And it is actively looking for a replacement, although nobody knows when Nvidia will find someone to step into the CEO role permanently. In my opinion, that's both good and bad.

It's bad because the longer this search drags on, the more uncertainty it could add to the company's prospects. But it's good because replacing a CEO as effective as Huang isn't an easy task, and the company's board is rightfully taking the time it needs to do so, or so it seems. In the meantime, several factors highlight just how massive an opportunity Nvidia could still tap into, even as it faces a more stringent regulatory environment.

During the recent U.S. midterm elections, voters elected many lawmakers and politicians across various states who had promised to be stricter on the AI industry. This may result in delayed permits and slower data center build-outs. However, Nvidia expects a great year ahead. The company raised its guidance for the fiscal year 2028, which covers most of the calendar year 2027.

The company now expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal year 2028, up from its previous projection of 70% -- and that's after also raising its guidance for its current fiscal year. If we assume Nvidia's fourth-quarter revenue lands at the midpoint, it could generate $423.7 billion this fiscal year and $741.4 billion next year, based on its projected 75% growth rate.

So, given its current market cap of $3.8 trillion, Nvidia is trading at 5.1x estimated fiscal year 2028 revenue -- that's more than fair for a company growing as fast as it is, in my view. However, the CEO search does introduce some uncertainty. And we still have to account for the risk of margin erosion as industry competition intensifies. So, what's the verdict?

Nvidia looks like a buy at current levels, but it's hardly a once-in-a-decade buying opportunity. Still, investors who purchase the company's shares today could see strong returns over the medium term.
